blocks.html: In World Geography you learned to read coordinates: every place on Earth has a latitude and a longitude. Human geography starts with a question that sounds simple: where is it? Geographers answer it in two ways, and each way tells you something different.

Absolute location is an exact position that never depends on anything else: coordinates (41.9° N, 87.6° W) or a street address. Relative location describes a place by its connections to other places: "on the southwest shore of Lake Michigan, where railroads from the East met the farms of the West."

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Chicago sits on Lake Michigan, between the farms of the Midwest and the cities of the East. That relative location helps explain why it grew.

blocks.html: Coordinates tell you where; relative location helps tell you why. In the 1800s, goods moved by water and rail. A spot where lake ships met railroads became a natural meeting point for grain, lumber and cattle from the West and factories and buyers in the East. Chicago's coordinates did not change while it grew from a small town into a giant city; its connections did.

blocks.title: Which kind is it?
blocks.q: Sort each description: (a) 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.; (b) "two blocks north of the train station"; (c) 51.5° N, 0.1° W.
steps: A street address names one exact spot in a system everyone shares, so (a) is absolute.
(b) only makes sense if you know where the train station is. It describes the place by its connection to another place, so it is relative.
(c) is a pair of coordinates, so it is absolute.
blocks.a: (a) absolute, (b) relative, (c) absolute.

blocks.title: Explaining a city with relative location
blocks.q: Singapore is a small island. Use relative location to explain why it became a busy port.
steps: Look at what is around it: Singapore lies at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula.
Ships sailing between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea pass through the narrow Strait of Malacca, right beside it.
A port on that route can serve ships traveling between Europe, South Asia and East Asia.
blocks.a: It sits beside one of the world's busiest sea lanes, so ships stop there to trade and refuel.

blocks.html: Many students think relative location is the "less exact" kind and therefore less useful. It is less exact, but it is often more useful. "Just south of the Great Lakes, on the main rail lines" explains why a city grew; "41.9° N, 87.6° W" does not. Check yourself: if a description mentions another place (a river, a road, a neighbor), it is relative.

blocks.html: Once you know absolute and relative location, you can ask why a settlement started at one spot and why it grew. Geographers split the answer into two parts: site and situation.

Site is the physical character of the place itself: its landforms, water supply, soil, climate and harbor. Situation is the place's location relative to other places: trade routes, neighbors, resources and markets nearby.

Early settlers chose sites for what the land offered on the spot: a hill that was easy to defend, an island in a river, fresh water, a sheltered harbor. But a good site alone rarely makes a big city. Cities grow large when their situation connects them to many other places, so goods, people and ideas pass through.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Singapore (orange dot) at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, beside the Strait of Malacca.

blocks.title: Paris
blocks.q: Paris began on an island in the Seine River. Its region later became the hub of France's roads and railways. Which fact is site and which is situation?
steps: An island in a river is a physical feature of the spot itself: it was easy to defend and to cross the river there. That is site.
Being the hub of the country's roads and railways describes how Paris connects to other places. That is situation.
blocks.a: Island in the Seine: site. Hub of roads and railways: situation.

blocks.title: New York City
blocks.q: Explain New York's growth using both ideas.
steps: Site: a deep, sheltered natural harbor at the mouth of the Hudson River.
Situation: after the Erie Canal opened in 1825, the Hudson and the canal linked the harbor to the Great Lakes and the farms of the interior.
A good site gave ships a safe place to dock; the situation gave them a huge region to trade with.
blocks.a: A fine harbor (site) plus a water route to the interior (situation).

blocks.html: Students often swap the two. A quick test: site is what you could see if you stood on the spot (the hill, the harbor, the river). Situation needs a bigger map, because it is about what lies around the spot: routes, neighbors and markets.

blocks.html: Situation can change. A port can lose ships to a new canal elsewhere, and a mountain town can boom when a ski resort or highway arrives. Its site stays nearly the same.

blocks.html: The world is too big to study one place at a time, so geographers group places into regions: areas that share something. What they share decides the kind of region. This builds on site and situation, which describe single places.

A formal region (uniform region) shares a measurable trait everywhere inside it, such as a language, a crop or a government. A functional region (nodal region) is tied to a central point, or node, by connections such as commuting, deliveries or broadcasts. A perceptual region (vernacular region) exists in people's minds; its borders differ from person to person.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Census Bureau's South: a formal region with exact borders drawn along state lines. "The South" that people picture is a perceptual region, and many would draw it differently.

blocks.html: The three kinds answer three questions. Formal: what is the same everywhere here? Functional: what is connected to this center? Perceptual: where do people think this place is? A functional region usually gets weaker toward its edges, because ties to the center fade with distance.

blocks.title: Three regions, three kinds
blocks.q: Name the kind: (a) the area where a city's newspaper is delivered; (b) the countries where Portuguese is an official language; (c) "the Midwest."
steps: (a) Everything in the area is linked to one center, the newspaper's office. That is functional.
(b) Every country in the group shares one trait, an official language. That is formal.
(c) People agree that the Midwest exists but disagree about where it ends. That is perceptual.
blocks.a: (a) functional, (b) formal, (c) perceptual.

blocks.title: A region with a hub that is still formal
blocks.q: A state has a capital city. Is the state a functional region because it has a hub?
steps: A state is defined by its legal border: the same laws apply everywhere inside it.
That shared trait makes it a formal region.
The capital does not define the border. If we drew a region by who commutes to the capital, that would be a functional region.
blocks.a: The state is formal; the capital's commuting area would be functional.

blocks.html: Students call any region with a hub a functional region, or any region with a city a formal one. Ask what defines the border. If the border comes from connections to a center (a TV station's viewers, an airport's flights, a pizza shop's delivery zone), the region is functional. If it comes from a trait shared everywhere, it is formal.

blocks.html: In World Geography, map scale meant the ratio between a distance on the map and the same distance on the ground. Human geographers also use the word scale in a second way, and mixing up the two is a classic trap.

The scale of analysis is the size of the area you study: global, regional (a group of countries or part of a country), national, or local. The same question can show different patterns at different scales.

blocks.name: humangeo-scale
blocks.cap: A made-up country seen at three scales. Switch from national to regional to local and watch the pattern appear.

blocks.html: An average blends many places into one number. At the national scale, a rich capital and a poor rural corner add up to "middle income." Zoom in to the regional or local scale and the differences show. Zoom out to the global scale and the country becomes one dot among many. No scale is the true one; each answers a different question.

blocks.title: Two meanings of scale
blocks.q: A student says, "A large-scale map shows the whole world." Is that right?
steps: On a map, "large scale" means a large ratio such as 1:10,000: things look big, so the map covers a small area.
A world map is small scale (such as 1:50,000,000).
Scale of analysis is different: studying the whole world is the global scale.
blocks.a: No. A world map is a small-scale map, even though it shows the global scale of analysis.

blocks.title: Choosing a scale
blocks.q: A city wants to know which neighborhoods need a new library. Which scale of analysis fits?
steps: The question is about differences inside one city.
National or global data would hide those differences.
Data by neighborhood or census tract fits the question.
blocks.a: The local scale.

blocks.html: Two errors are common. First, confusing map scale (a ratio) with scale of analysis (how big an area you study). Second, assuming a pattern at one scale holds at every scale. A country can look rich at the national scale and still have very poor regions; a poor country can have a wealthy capital. Check: before you draw a conclusion, say which scale your data describes.

blocks.html: Think about where you went last week. Most trips were probably short: school, a store, a friend's house. Long trips were rare. That everyday pattern is one of the oldest ideas in geography, and it explains how ideas and goods spread, which you will see again in How Things Spread.

Distance decay: interaction between places falls off as the distance between them grows. Time-space compression: faster, cheaper travel and communication make distant places feel closer, so the decay becomes weaker.

blocks.name: humangeo-decay
blocks.cap: The share of trips by distance. Move the slider to see what faster travel does.

blocks.html: Every trip, phone call or shipment costs time, money or effort, and the cost grows with distance. So people make many short trips and few long ones. The geographer Waldo Tobler put it this way in 1970: everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things. The geographer David Harvey used the term time-space compression (1989) for how railroads, jets and now the internet have shrunk those costs.

blocks.title: Reading a decay pattern
blocks.q: A grocery store finds that 60% of its shoppers live within 2 km, 25% live 2 to 5 km away, and 15% live farther. What does this show?
steps: The share of shoppers falls as distance grows.
That is distance decay.
The store's customers form a functional region around it that weakens toward the edges.
blocks.a: Distance decay: most shoppers come from nearby.

blocks.title: Time-space compression
blocks.q: In 1850 a letter from New York to San Francisco took weeks; today an email arrives in seconds. What changed, and what did not?
steps: The time to send a message fell almost to zero: that is time-space compression.
The distance in kilometers stayed exactly the same.
What changed is the cost of crossing that distance.
blocks.a: Communication became nearly instant, so the two cities feel closer, but their distance did not change.

blocks.html: Many students think distance no longer matters because of the internet. It still does. Most trips, most trade between countries and most migration are still between places that are fairly close. Time-space compression weakens distance decay; it does not erase it. Studies of phone calls and online friendships still find the most contact between nearby places.

blocks.html: When geographers look at a map of houses, stores or farms, they describe the arrangement with three words that are easy to confuse: density, concentration and pattern. This lesson builds on scales of analysis: each of these depends on the area you choose.

Density is how many things there are per unit of area (houses per square mile). Concentration is how close together they are: clustered (bunched) or dispersed (spread out). Pattern is the geometric arrangement: clustered, dispersed, random, or linear (along a line such as a road or river).

blocks.name: humangeo-pattern
blocks.cap: Same number of houses, same area: the density is the same. The concentration is not.

blocks.html: Density is a single number: a count divided by an area. It says nothing about where inside the area the things are. Two squares with 24 houses in 4 square miles both have 6 houses per square mile, even if one has all its houses in two tight clusters. Concentration and pattern describe that arrangement, which density cannot.

blocks.title: Computing density
blocks.q: A township of 36 square miles has 540 farms. What is its density of farms?
steps: Density = number ÷ area.
Write the units: farms per square mile.
blocks.a: 15 farms per square mile.

blocks.title: Same density, different concentration
blocks.q: Town A and Town B each have 200 houses on 10 square miles. In A the houses line a main street; in B they are spread evenly over the land. Compare them.
steps: Density: 200 ÷ 10 = 20 houses per square mile in both.
Concentration: A's houses are clustered along one street; B's are dispersed.
Pattern: A is linear; B is dispersed.
blocks.a: Same density; A is clustered in a linear pattern, B is dispersed.

blocks.name: humangeo-pattern
blocks.cap: A random pattern, and a linear pattern along a road.

blocks.html: Students treat density and concentration as the same thing. They are not: changing where houses sit inside a square changes the concentration but not the density. Check: if you can compute it by dividing a count by an area, it is density; if you are describing how bunched or spread out things are, it is concentration.

blocks.html: Geographers study patterns like density and concentration, but where do the facts come from? In GPS, GIS and Satellite Images you saw some of the tools. This lesson sorts the data itself into two kinds and asks what each is good for.

Quantitative data are numbers: census counts, incomes, temperatures, satellite measurements of land cover. Qualitative data are words, pictures and observations: interviews, photographs, field notes, travel diaries. Good geography often uses both: numbers show what and where; words and pictures help explain why.

blocks.html: A map of numbers can show that a neighborhood lost half its stores in ten years, but not why. Talking with shop owners and residents, or photographing empty storefronts, can reveal causes the numbers miss: a new highway, rising rents, a mall built nearby. Numbers let you compare many places fairly; words and pictures let you understand one place deeply.

items: Censuses: counts of a whole population, often every ten years (the U.S. census since 1790).
Surveys: questions asked of a sample of people.
Remote sensing: data gathered from satellites, planes and drones, without visiting.
Fieldwork: observing, measuring, photographing and interviewing on the spot.
GIS (geographic information systems): software that layers many kinds of data on one map.

blocks.title: Choosing data
blocks.q: You want to learn why young people are leaving a rural county. Which data would you gather?
steps: Quantitative: census counts by age over several decades show how many left and when.
Qualitative: interviews with young people and their parents show the reasons, such as jobs or schools.
Together they show both the size of the change and its causes.
blocks.a: Both: census numbers for the pattern, interviews for the reasons.

blocks.title: Is a survey quantitative?
blocks.q: A survey asks, "In your own words, what do you like about this town?" What kind of data does it give?
steps: The answers are open-ended words, not numbers.
So they are qualitative, even though they come from a survey.
blocks.a: Qualitative.

blocks.html: Students think only numbers count as data. Interviews, photos and field notes are data too, collected and recorded carefully. The kind of data depends on its form (numbers or words and images), not on whether it came from a computer or a survey.

blocks.html: On a choropleth map the eye reads area: big, dark regions look important. If you shade by totals, large regions get dark just because they are large and hold more people. A rate divides by area (or by population), which removes that size effect, so the shading compares places fairly.

blocks.title: Matching data to maps
blocks.q: Choose a map for each: (a) the number of passengers at 30 airports; (b) the percent of adults with a college degree in each state; (c) average January temperature.
steps: (a) Totals at points: graduated symbols.
(b) A percentage for each area: a choropleth.
(c) A value that changes smoothly across the land: isolines.
blocks.a: (a) graduated symbols, (b) choropleth, (c) isolines.

blocks.title: Fixing a map
blocks.q: A student shades U.S. states by total number of farms. Texas is darkest. What is the problem and the fix?
steps: Texas is huge, so it has many farms partly because it has so much land.
Shading by totals makes big states look important.
Fix: shade by a rate (farms per 1,000 km², or percent of land in farms), or show totals with graduated symbols.
blocks.a: Use a rate on the choropleth, or graduated symbols for the totals.

blocks.html: The most common thematic-map mistake is a choropleth of raw totals. Check: does the legend have "per" or "percent" in it? If not, and the map shades areas, it probably should use a rate instead.

blocks.html: People shape the land, and the land shapes what people can do. Since site and situation showed how physical features help a place grow, a bigger question follows: how much does the environment decide how people live? Geographers have answered it in different ways over time.

Environmental determinism said the physical environment, especially climate, decides how people and societies behave. Possibilism says the environment sets limits and offers possibilities, and people choose among them using their culture and technology. Today geographers study human-environment interaction: how people and environments shape each other, and which uses of land and resources are sustainable.

Determinism was popular around 1900 (the American geographers Ellen Churchill Semple and Ellsworth Huntington were well-known supporters). It fell apart because it could not explain why people in the same environment live very differently, or why societies change while their climate stays the same. It also claimed that some climates made some peoples better than others, ideas that were used to justify ranking and ruling peoples. The French geographer Paul Vidal de la Blache stressed people's ways of life instead, and the historian Lucien Febvre named the idea possibilism (1922).

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Netherlands (orange). About a quarter of the country lies below sea level; dikes, pumps and drained land called polders made it farmland and cities.

blocks.title: Which view is it?
blocks.q: "People in hot climates are lazy, so hot countries will always be poor." Which view is this, and why do geographers reject it?
steps: It claims climate decides behavior and wealth: environmental determinism.
It ignores history, trade, policy and technology, which differ among countries with the same climate.
Hot countries such as Singapore are rich, and many cool countries have been poor; climate does not decide the outcome.
blocks.a: Environmental determinism; the evidence does not support it, and it was used to rank peoples unfairly.

blocks.title: Possibilism in action
blocks.q: The Netherlands drained shallow seas and marshes to make farmland. How does possibilism describe this?
steps: The environment set a limit: low, wet land often flooded by the sea.
People chose a response using technology: dikes, windmills and later pumps.
The same environment could have led to other choices, such as fishing or moving away.
blocks.a: The environment offered limits and options; Dutch society chose to reclaim land.

blocks.html: Students sometimes present environmental determinism as an accepted explanation. Geographers set it aside long ago: it ignored culture and choice, and it was used to rank peoples unfairly. You should know it as a historical idea. That does not mean the environment does not matter. Rainfall, soil and slope do limit farming; the point is that people respond in many different ways.

blocks.html: In Eight Billion People you learned that about 8.2 billion people lived on Earth in 2024 (UN). They are not spread evenly. A few regions hold most of humanity, and huge areas hold almost no one. Using location and the physical map, you can explain why.

Most people live in four clusters: East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia and Europe. Nearly 60 percent of the world's people live in Asia (UN, 2025). People crowd onto low, well-watered land with good soil and a mild climate, often near coasts and rivers. Very dry, very cold, very high and very wet places have few people.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Orange: some of the most crowded countries. Blue: very large countries with few people for their size.

blocks.html: For most of history nearly everyone farmed, and farming needs flat land, water, good soil and a growing season. River valleys and deltas, such as the Ganges in South Asia and the Yangtze in China, gave all of these and could feed dense populations. Places that cannot be farmed easily, such as the Sahara, Siberia, the Australian outback and high mountains, stayed thinly settled, and they still are. The part of Earth where people live permanently is called the ecumene.

blocks.title: Size is not population
blocks.q: Canada's land area is roughly 70 times Bangladesh's, yet Bangladesh has several times as many people. Why?
steps: Most of Canada is cold: forests and tundra with short growing seasons. Most Canadians live in a narrow band near the U.S. border.
Bangladesh lies on the warm, wet, fertile delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers.
Fertile, warm land can feed many people on a small area.
blocks.a: Bangladesh's land is warm, wet and fertile; most of Canada is too cold to farm.

blocks.title: Where in Egypt?
blocks.q: Egypt is about one million square kilometers, mostly desert. Where would you expect its people to live?
steps: Water is the limiting factor in a desert.
The Nile River brings water and fertile soil through the desert.
So people crowd into the Nile valley and delta: over 95 percent of Egyptians live there.
blocks.a: Along the Nile valley and in its delta.

blocks.html: Students assume population follows country size. Russia, Canada and Australia are among the largest countries but hold few people for their size; small, fertile river valleys and deltas can be crowded. Check a population claim against the physical map: where are the water, the flat land and the growing season?

blocks.html: In Crowded Places you found population density: people divided by land area. That single number can mislead, because not all land can feed people. Geographers use three densities, and the difference between them is which people and which land you count.

head: Density
Divide
By
blocks.cap: Three densities: which people, and which land.

items: Arithmetic tells how crowded the country is overall.
Physiological tells how much pressure people put on farmland.
Agricultural tells how many farmers work each piece of farmland.

blocks.name: humangeo-density
blocks.cap: A made-up country where only a tenth of the land can be farmed. Switch between the three densities.

blocks.html: Physiological density = people ÷ arable land. When it is much higher than arithmetic density, most of the country's land cannot be farmed. Agricultural density = farmers ÷ arable land. High agricultural density usually means farming uses many hands and few machines.

People eat food grown on farmland, not on deserts or ice. Dividing by arable land measures how many mouths each square kilometer of farmland must support. Rich countries often have low agricultural density even when physiological density is high, because a few farmers with machines work large areas.

blocks.title: All three densities
blocks.q: A country has 200,000 km² of land, of which 10% is arable. It has 30 million people, and 9 million of them farm. Find the three densities.
steps: Arable land = 10% of 200,000 = 20,000 km².
Arithmetic: 30,000,000 ÷ 200,000 = 150 people per km².
Physiological: 30,000,000 ÷ 20,000 = 1,500 people per km² of farmland.
Agricultural: 9,000,000 ÷ 20,000 = 450 farmers per km² of farmland.
blocks.a: 150, 1,500 and 450 per km².

blocks.title: Reading the gap
blocks.q: Country X: arithmetic density 50, physiological density 1,000. Country Y: arithmetic 50, physiological 120. What does the gap tell you?
steps: Same people per km² of all land.
X has far more people per km² of farmland, so little of its land is arable (50 ÷ 1,000 = 5%).
Y has much more farmland (50 ÷ 120 ≈ 42%).
blocks.a: X has little arable land and much more pressure on it.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Egypt: a large desert country whose farmland is a thin strip along the Nile. Its physiological density is many times its arithmetic density.

blocks.html: The usual error is dividing by the wrong land area. Physiological and agricultural density divide by arable land only, never by total land. And agricultural density counts farmers only, not everyone. Check: physiological density must always be at least as large as arithmetic density, because arable land is part of all land.

blocks.html: A population changes in only four ways: births and immigrants add people; deaths and emigrants subtract them. Demographers start with births and deaths. Because countries differ hugely in size, they compare rates, not raw counts, using the idea of a percent and its cousin, "per 1,000."

The crude birth rate (CBR) is births per 1,000 people in a year. The crude death rate (CDR) is deaths per 1,000 people in a year. The rate of natural increase (RNI) is CBR − CDR, usually written as a percent: divide the difference by 10.

"Per 1,000" is a fraction with 1,000 on the bottom; a percent has 100 on the bottom. So 20 per 1,000 = 2 per 100 = 2%. That is why you divide by 10. The word natural means the rate leaves out migration: it counts only births and deaths. And crude means the rates use the whole population, of every age, as the base.

blocks.name: gg-dtm
blocks.cap: Birth and death rates over the demographic transition. Move through time and watch the gap between the lines: that gap is natural increase.

blocks.title: From counts to rates
blocks.q: A country of 4,000,000 people had 96,000 births and 28,000 deaths last year. Find CBR, CDR and RNI.
steps: Difference: 24 − 7 = 17 per 1,000.
As a percent: 17 ÷ 10 = 1.7%.
blocks.a: CBR 24, CDR 7, RNI 1.7% a year.

blocks.title: A shrinking population

Check the size: a 20% growth rate would double a population in under four years, which no country does. Real natural increase rates are between about −1% and 4%.

blocks.html: The crude birth rate depends on how many people of childbearing age a country has. Demographers want measures that compare countries fairly and say something about families and health. Three are used everywhere.

The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime at today's rates. Replacement level is about 2.1 in countries with low death rates. The infant mortality rate (IMR) is deaths of babies under one year per 1,000 live births. Life expectancy is the average number of years a newborn would live at today's death rates.

Two parents need to be replaced by two children who grow up to have children of their own. It takes slightly more than 2.0, because a few children die before adulthood and slightly more boys than girls are born (about 105 boys per 100 girls). Where more children die young, replacement level is higher than 2.1. The infant mortality rate divides by births, not by the whole population, so it measures how safe the first year of life is.

items: World TFR: about 2.3 children per woman (UN, 2024); more than half of all countries and areas are below 2.1.
World life expectancy at birth: about 73.3 years (UN, 2024).

blocks.cap: High fertility gives a wide base of young children; low fertility gives a narrow one.

blocks.title: Infant mortality
blocks.q: A region had 50,000 live births in a year, and 1,200 babies died before their first birthday. Find the IMR.
steps: IMR = infant deaths ÷ live births × 1,000.
blocks.a: 24 infant deaths per 1,000 live births.

blocks.title: Above or below replacement?
blocks.q: Country A has a TFR of 1.4; Country B has 3.8. What does each suggest, ignoring migration?
steps: A is below 2.1: each generation is smaller than its parents' generation, so in the long run the population shrinks.
B is well above 2.1: each generation is larger, so the population grows.
Neither changes overnight: an age structure takes decades to catch up.
blocks.a: A: long-run decline; B: growth.

blocks.html: Students think a TFR of 2.0 keeps a population steady. Two children per woman falls just short, because not every child survives to have children and more boys than girls are born. Replacement is about 2.1 in rich countries and higher where child deaths are common. Also, a low TFR does not mean a population shrinks at once; that depends on its age structure.

blocks.html: If a population grows 2 percent a year, how long until it doubles? Because growth builds on growth, like interest on savings, the answer is shorter than 50 years. A simple rule, using the rate of natural increase, gives a good estimate.
The rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate, with the rate written as a percent (2, not 0.02). At 2% a year, doubling takes about 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years.

Each year the population is multiplied by (1 + r). Doubling means (1 + r)<sup>n</sup> = 2. Taking natural logarithms, n = ln 2 ÷ ln(1 + r). For small r, ln(1 + r) is very close to r, and ln 2 ≈ 0.693. So n ≈ 0.693 ÷ r = 69.3 ÷ (r as a percent). Rounding 69.3 up to 70 makes the arithmetic easy.

blocks.name: gg-dtm
blocks.cap: In stage 2 the gap between birth and death rates is widest, so doubling time is shortest.

blocks.title: Doubling time from a rate
blocks.q: A country's RNI is 2.5% a year. About how long will it take to double?
steps: Use the percent: 2.5.
blocks.a: About 28 years.

blocks.title: From birth and death rates
blocks.q: CBR 31 per 1,000, CDR 7 per 1,000. Find the doubling time.
blocks.a: About 29 years.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: A city doubled in about 20 years. What was its yearly growth rate?
steps: Rule of 70: rate ≈ 70 ÷ doubling time.
blocks.a: About 3.5% a year.

blocks.html: Students divide 70 by the decimal (70 ÷ 0.02 = 3,500 years). Use the percent: 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years. Check the size: at 2% a year, simple addition would take 50 years to add 100%, and compounding makes it a bit faster, so the answer must be somewhat under 50. Remember too that the rule assumes the rate stays the same, which real populations rarely do.

blocks.html: Birth, death and fertility rates leave a fingerprint on a population: how many people there are of each age. A population pyramid draws that fingerprint.

A population pyramid is two bar graphs back to back: males on the left, females on the right. Each bar is one age group (0–4, 5–9, …), youngest at the bottom. The length of a bar is the share of the whole population (or the number of people) in that group today.

blocks.name: gg-pyramid
blocks.cap: Change how fast births grow and how high death rates are, and watch the shape change.

blocks.html: Everyone in the 40–44 bar was born 40 to 44 years ago, so each bar records a past group of births, minus the people who have since died or moved away, plus those who moved in. Read upward and you are reading backward in time. A wide bar at 20–24 above narrower bars below means births have fallen in the last twenty years.

blocks.title: Reading a bar
blocks.q: On a pyramid, the 10–14 bar shows 6% male and 5.8% female. What share of the population is 10 to 14 years old?
steps: Add the two sides: 6 + 5.8 = 11.8.
Each side is a share of the whole population, so the total is 11.8%.
blocks.a: 11.8% of the population.

blocks.title: Under 15
blocks.q: The bars for 0–4, 5–9 and 10–14 total 8%, 7.5% and 7% (both sexes). What share is under 15?
steps: Under 15 means the three youngest groups: 0–4, 5–9 and 10–14.

blocks.html: Students read the bars as births each year, or as the number of people who died. Each bar is how many people of that age are alive now. A narrow base means few young children today, which usually means fewer births in recent years. Check: the bars of a percentage pyramid add up to 100%.

blocks.name: gg-pyramid
blocks.cap: The highlighted bars are people aged 15 to 64, the ages when most people work.

blocks.html: Once you can read a population pyramid, the overall shape tells a story at a glance. Geographers sort the shapes into three families.

blocks.name: gg-pyramid
blocks.cap: Three shapes: expanding, stable and contracting.

blocks.html: Expanding (wide base, narrow top): many births, many deaths at each age, fast growth. Stable (straight sides, like a column): births and deaths roughly balanced, slow or no growth. Contracting (base narrower than the middle): few births, an aging population that may shrink.

The base shows recent births; the slope of the sides shows how fast each group thins out from deaths. A wide base and steep taper mean high birth rates and high death rates at every age. Straight sides mean few people die before old age and births have been steady. A narrow base under a wide middle means births dropped below the level of earlier decades.

blocks.title: Naming a shape
blocks.q: A pyramid has its widest bars at ages 35–49, and each bar below is narrower. What shape is it, and what does it say?
steps: The base is narrower than the middle.
That is a contracting pyramid.
Births have fallen for decades; the population is aging and may shrink unless people move in.
blocks.a: Contracting: an aging population with low birth rates.

blocks.title: A bulge
blocks.q: A pyramid has one unusually wide band of bars around ages 60–75. What might cause it?
steps: A wide band means many people were born in those years.
Many countries had a baby boom after World War II; in the United States it lasted from about 1946 to 1964.
Those babies are now in their 60s and 70s.
blocks.a: A past baby boom moving up the pyramid.

blocks.html: Students think a narrow base always means the country is shrinking today. Not necessarily. Immigration can add working-age adults, and a population with few children can keep growing for years because many people are of childbearing age (this is called population momentum). Read the shape as a clue to the past and a likely future, not a certain one.

titles: A stable population with many working-age migrants

blocks.cap: Migrants can add a bulge in the working ages.

blocks.html: A population pyramid shows who might be working and who might need support. The dependency ratio puts that into one number, using percents of a number.
Dependency ratio = (people aged 0–14 + people aged 65 and over) ÷ people aged 15–64 × 100. It is the number of dependents for every 100 people of working age.

blocks.name: gg-pyramid
blocks.cap: An expanding pyramid. The highlighted bars are children under 15. The readout gives the dependency ratio.

blocks.html: Children under 15 are mostly in school, and many people over 65 have retired. Their food, schooling, health care and pensions are paid for largely by people of working age, through families and taxes. The ratio is only a rough guide: many teenagers and older people work, and many adults do not.

blocks.title: From percents
blocks.q: A country is 38% under 15, 3% over 64, and 59% aged 15 to 64. Find the dependency ratio.
steps: Dependents: 38 + 3 = 41.
Working age: 59.
blocks.a: About 69 dependents per 100 people of working age.

blocks.title: Young and old
blocks.q: Country A: 15% under 15, 25% over 64. Country B: 35% under 15, 5% over 64. Compare their dependency ratios.
steps: Both have 40% dependents and 60% working age.
But A's dependents are mostly old (pensions, health care) and B's are mostly young (schools).
blocks.a: Equal ratios (about 67), with very different needs.

blocks.title: From counts
blocks.q: A town has 1,800 children under 15, 1,200 people over 64 and 6,000 people aged 15 to 64. Find the ratio.

blocks.html: Students count only the elderly as dependents. Children under 15 count too, so countries with many children (expanding pyramids) often have high dependency ratios, just like aging countries. Also, the ratio divides by the working-age group, not by the whole population. Check: if the answer is "percent of the population," you divided by the wrong number.

blocks.html: Put birth and death rates on one graph over two centuries and a pattern appears in country after country. The American demographer Warren Thompson described it in 1929, and Frank Notestein and others developed it into the demographic transition model (DTM).

blocks.name: gg-dtm
blocks.cap: Move through the stages and read the birth rate, death rate and growth at each point.

blocks.html: As countries develop, death rates fall first (better food, clean water, medicine), and birth rates fall later (cities, schooling, jobs for women, children surviving). The gap in between is when the population grows fastest.

Death rates can fall quickly because nearly everyone wants to live longer, and vaccines or clean water spread fast. Birth rates depend on family choices shaped by culture and economics, which change more slowly. Families have many children where children work on farms and many die young; they choose fewer where children survive, cost more to raise and need long schooling.

blocks.title: Placing a country
blocks.q: CBR 34 per 1,000, CDR 8 per 1,000. Which stage fits?
steps: Death rate is already low; birth rate is still high.
RNI = (34 − 8) ÷ 10 = 2.6%: fast growth.
High births with low deaths and fast growth is stage 2 (moving toward 3).
blocks.a: Stage 2.

blocks.title: Another country
blocks.q: CBR 10, CDR 11. Which stage?
steps: Births are below deaths.
Natural decrease of 0.1% a year.
blocks.a: Stage 5 (declining).

blocks.html: Students think the population grows fastest in stage 1, "when birth rates are highest." Growth depends on the gap between births and deaths, not on births alone. In stage 1 both are high, so the gap is small. Growth is fastest in stage 2, when deaths have fallen but births have not. Also remember that the DTM was built from the history of Europe and North America; countries may move through it faster, slower or differently, and it does not include migration.

blocks.html: The demographic transition shows death rates falling. The epidemiological transition, described by the physician Abdel Omran in 1971, asks what people die of at each stage.

As countries develop, the main causes of death shift from infectious diseases, famine and childbirth (spread by germs, bad water and poor nutrition) to chronic and degenerative diseases such as heart disease, stroke and cancer, which strike mostly older people.

blocks.html: Infectious diseases kill people of every age, especially babies and children. Clean water, sewers, vaccines, antibiotics and better food prevent most of those deaths. People then live long enough that the diseases of old age become the leading causes. Everyone dies of something, and in a country where few die young, that something is usually a chronic disease.

blocks.title: Placing a pattern
blocks.q: In a country, the top causes of death are heart disease, stroke and cancer, and life expectancy is over 80. Which stage?
steps: Chronic, degenerative diseases lead.
Life expectancy is very high, so they strike late in life.
blocks.a: Stage 4 (delayed degenerative diseases).

blocks.title: Why cholera faded
blocks.q: Cholera spreads through dirty water. Why did it stop being a leading cause of death in many cities?
steps: Cities built clean water supplies and sewers in the 1800s and 1900s.
Without dirty water, cholera could not spread.
That is the move from stage 1 to stage 2.
blocks.a: Clean water and sewers cut its spread.

blocks.html: Students think chronic diseases became common because people became less healthy. Mostly they lead because people now live long enough to get them. A disease of old age cannot be common where few reach old age. Diet and smoking matter too, but the main reason is that the deaths of the young have been prevented.

blocks.html: In stage 2 of the demographic transition, populations grow fast. Can food keep up? This question has been argued for more than two centuries, and it is still debated. Your job is to know each side's argument, not to pick a winner.

In An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), Thomas Malthus argued that population tends to grow faster than the food supply, so hunger, disease and war (or later marriage and fewer births) would hold numbers down. Critics point to food output that has grown faster than population and to falling birth rates. Neo-Malthusians warn that limits on water, land, energy and the environment still matter.

Malthus said population could grow geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8, …) while food could grow only arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4, …). If that were true, population would always outrun food. So far, farm output has kept ahead: new crop varieties, fertilizer, irrigation and machines raised yields, and birth rates fell in most countries. The Danish economist Ester Boserup (1965) argued that growing populations push farmers to farm more intensively. Neo-Malthusians, such as the biologist Paul Ehrlich in The Population Bomb (1968), answered that today's gains may use up soil, water and fossil fuels faster than they can be replaced.

blocks.html: Students treat Malthus as either proven right or simply wrong. His prediction of permanent mass famine has not come true for the world as a whole, because food output grew faster than he expected. But scholars still debate whether limits on water, land and the environment will matter in the future. On an exam, give each side's argument and its evidence.

blocks.html: The debate over population growth is not only an argument among scholars. Governments have tried to change their populations, sometimes to slow growth and sometimes to speed it up. Geographers sort these policies into three kinds.

Antinatalist policies try to lower birth rates (family planning, limits on family size). Pronatalist policies try to raise birth rates (payments for children, paid parental leave, child care). Immigration policies decide how many people may move in, and who.

Family allowances, paid parental leave and public child care.
A points system that scores applicants on education, skills and language.

blocks.html: Countries with fast growth may worry about feeding, schooling and employing a growing population. Countries with low fertility worry about a shrinking workforce paying for many retirees (a high dependency ratio). Immigration can add working-age people quickly, which is why some low-fertility countries welcome immigrants while others limit them.

blocks.q: A country has a TFR of 1.3 and an aging population. Which kinds of policy might it consider?

To raise births: pronatalist policies such as child care and parental leave.
To add workers sooner: more immigration.

blocks.html: Students think governments can set birth rates easily. Results are mixed. Birth rates in many countries fell without any policy, as people moved to cities and stayed in school longer, and pronatalist payments have often raised births only a little. Education, jobs, housing costs and the cost of raising children often matter more. Whether and how governments should try is debated; know the arguments on each side.

blocks.html: Why did fertility fall in so many countries, often without any population policy? One of the strongest patterns in population geography links fertility to girls' schooling and women's work.

Where more girls finish secondary school and more women work for pay, women tend to marry later and have fewer children, later in life. This pattern holds across regions and religions, though the size of the effect varies.

Several things happen together. Years in school delay marriage and first births. Education raises what a woman can earn, so time away from paid work costs more. Educated parents often know more about health and family planning, and their children are more likely to survive, so families need fewer births to reach the size they want. Cities, where schooling and paid work are easier to find, push the same way: children cost more there and are less often needed on a farm.

blocks.title: Reading a pattern
blocks.q: In a set of regions, the share of women with secondary schooling rises from 20% to 80%, and TFR falls from 5.5 to 2.0. What can you conclude?
steps: The two measures move in opposite directions: a negative correlation.
That fits the pattern, but correlation alone does not prove one causes the other.
Other changes, such as cities and health care, often rise along with schooling.
blocks.a: More schooling goes with lower fertility; schooling is likely one of several causes.

blocks.title: Two explanations
blocks.q: Give two reasons girls' schooling could lower fertility.
steps: Staying in school delays marriage and first births.
Education raises earnings, so having many children costs more in lost income.
blocks.a: Later marriage and higher earnings (also better health knowledge).

blocks.html: Students reverse cause and effect, or assume one factor explains everything. It is true both that schooling tends to lower fertility and that having fewer children can make it easier for women to stay in school and work. Schooling, health care, cities and jobs usually change together, so researchers try to separate their effects. Say "is associated with" unless you have evidence about cause.

blocks.html: Births and deaths are two ways a population changes; migration is the third. Migration is a permanent or long-term move to a new home. Because it changes where people live, geographers sort migrations by where people go and why.

Internal migration stays within one country (from a farm to a city, from one state to another); international migration crosses a border. Voluntary migrants choose to move; forced migrants are made to move or must flee. Chain migration follows family and friends who moved earlier. Step migration happens in stages (village → town → city).

items: Emigration: leaving a country. Immigration: arriving in one. Net migration = immigrants − emigrants.
Transhumance: herders moving animals between summer and winter pastures each year.
Guest workers: people allowed into a country to work for a limited time.
Rural-to-urban migration: the largest internal flow in most developing countries.

blocks.name: gg-diffusion
blocks.cap: When people move, they carry their culture with them.

blocks.html: Geographers sort migrations because each kind has different causes and effects. A forced move happens suddenly and often without a choice of destination, so it needs a different response than a planned move for a job. Internal moves reshape a country's own map, while international moves change two countries at once. Chain and step migration explain the routes people take: newcomers go where family can help them, or move a step at a time as they save money and gain experience.

blocks.title: Classifying moves
blocks.q: Classify: (a) the Great Migration, when millions of African Americans moved from the rural South to cities of the North and West (about 1910 to 1970); (b) the Atlantic slave trade.
steps: (a) Within the United States, so internal. People chose to move for jobs and to escape discrimination, so voluntary, though push factors were strong. Many followed relatives: chain migration.
(b) Millions of Africans were captured and carried across the ocean against their will: international and forced.
blocks.a: (a) internal, voluntary, often chain; (b) international, forced.

blocks.title: Step migration
blocks.q: A young woman moves from her village to a market town for school, then to the capital for work. What kind of migration?
steps: She moves in stages, each to a larger place.
That is step migration (and internal, rural-to-urban).
blocks.a: Step migration.

blocks.html: Students count refugees as voluntary migrants because they "decided to leave." People fleeing war, persecution or disaster are forced migrants: staying was not a safe choice. Also, internal migration counts as migration even though no border is crossed; it is in fact far more common than international migration.

blocks.html: Every migration involves two places: the one left behind and the one chosen. The demographer Everett Lee (1966) described migration as a weighing of factors at both ends, with obstacles in between.

Push factors are reasons to leave the place of origin (war, few jobs, drought, persecution). Pull factors are reasons to go to a destination (jobs, safety, schools, family). Intervening obstacles stand in between (distance, cost, borders and visas, mountains, language). An intervening opportunity is a closer place that offers the same pull, so the migrant stops there.

People rarely move for one reason. A farmer whose crops failed (push) may still stay unless a city offers work (pull) and the trip is affordable (no big obstacle). Factors are often grouped as economic (jobs, wages), social and cultural (family, religion, schools), political (war, freedom, laws) and environmental (drought, floods, climate).

head: Push (origin)
Pull (destination)

blocks.title: Sorting factors
blocks.q: A family leaves a drought-stricken farm and moves to a city where an uncle runs a business. Name the push, the pull and a possible obstacle.
steps: Push (about the place left): the drought.
Pull (about the place chosen): the uncle and his business, so family and a job.
Obstacle: the cost of the move or the distance.
blocks.a: Push: drought. Pull: family and work. Obstacle: cost or distance.

blocks.title: The Dust Bowl
blocks.q: In the 1930s, drought and dust storms struck the southern Great Plains. Many families moved to California. Classify the factors.
steps: Drought and failed farms on the Plains: environmental and economic push factors.
Hoped-for farm jobs and a mild climate in California: economic and environmental pull factors.
The long, costly road west was an intervening obstacle.
blocks.a: Environmental and economic push; economic pull; distance as an obstacle.

blocks.html: Students sort a factor by whether it is good or bad. "Jobs in another country" is a pull; "no jobs at home" is a push. Ask: is this about the place being left, or the place being chosen? Good things at the destination pull; bad things at the origin push.

blocks.html: Long before Everett Lee wrote about push and pull factors, the geographer Ernst Georg Ravenstein studied British census records and published "The Laws of Migration" (in 1885 and 1889). His "laws" are really patterns, and several still hold.

items: Most migrants move only a short distance.
Migrants who go long distances usually head for big cities.
Each migration flow produces a smaller counterflow in the opposite direction.
Most migration happens in steps.
People in rural areas are more likely to migrate than people in cities.
In his data, women were more likely than men to migrate within the country, and men more likely to move abroad.
Most migration is for economic reasons.

blocks.html: Ravenstein's main idea is distance decay applied to migration: most migrants move short distances, often within their own country or region, while long-distance migrants tend to head for large cities.

blocks.name: humangeo-decay
blocks.cap: The share of migrants by distance moved: most moves are short.

blocks.html: Short moves cost less, carry less risk and keep people near family. People know more about nearby places, so they find jobs and homes there more easily. A big city draws people from far away because it offers so many jobs that the long trip is worth it. Counterflows happen because some migrants return home, and news and connections flow back along the same path, drawing a few people the other way.

blocks.title: Which law?
blocks.q: For every 10 people who move from a rural state to a big coastal city, about 3 move from that city to the rural state. Which pattern is this?
steps: There is a main flow and a smaller flow in the other direction.
That is a counterflow.
blocks.a: Each flow produces a counterflow.

blocks.title: Testing a claim
blocks.q: A student says most migrants cross oceans. What would Ravenstein say?
steps: He found most migrants move short distances.
Today, too, many more people move within their own country than between countries.
blocks.a: Most migrants move short distances, usually within their own country.

blocks.html: Because news focuses on international migration, students expect most migrants to cross oceans or borders. Most people who move stay in their own country, often in their own region. Long-distance moves are the exception, and they usually end in large cities. Remember too that Ravenstein's laws describe tendencies in 1880s Britain; test them against other times and places rather than treating them as rules.

blocks.html: Among forced migrants, international law draws careful lines. The words refugee, asylum seeker and internally displaced person are often mixed up, but each has a precise meaning that decides what protection a person can receive.

A refugee has fled their own country and cannot safely return because of a well-founded fear of persecution (the 1951 Refugee Convention lists race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group and political opinion). An asylum seeker has asked another country for protection, but the claim has not yet been decided. An internally displaced person (IDP) was forced from home but is still inside their own country.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: Fled persecution to a neighboring country and was granted protection
Fled fighting to a safer city in the same country
Applied for protection at a border; the case is still being heard
Left a flooded region for relatives in another province

cards.text: Recognized by the UN refugee agency in a camp abroad

blocks.html: The lines matter because they decide who is responsible. A refugee is outside their country, so international refugee law applies, including the principle of non-refoulement: a refugee should not be sent back to a place where they face serious danger. An IDP is still inside their own country, so that country's government remains responsible for them; the UN's Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement (1998) set out their rights but are not a treaty. An asylum seeker's status is waiting on a decision: some will be recognized as refugees and some will not.

blocks.title: Same cause, different status
blocks.q: War breaks out in a country. Family A flees to the capital, which is still safe. Family B crosses the border and applies for protection. What is each family's status?
steps: Family A never left its country: internally displaced persons.
Family B crossed a border and applied for protection, but has no decision yet: asylum seekers.
If B's claim is accepted, B will be recognized as refugees.
blocks.a: A: IDPs. B: asylum seekers (refugees once recognized).

blocks.title: Is every migrant a refugee?
blocks.q: A worker moves abroad because wages are higher there. Is the worker a refugee?
steps: The move is for economic reasons, not to escape persecution.
The worker could return home safely.
blocks.a: No: a voluntary economic migrant.

blocks.html: Students use "refugee" for anyone who fled. If people never left their own country, they are internally displaced, not refugees, even if they fled the same war. And a person who has asked for protection but not yet received a decision is an asylum seeker. Check two questions: Did they cross an international border? Has their claim been decided?

blocks.html: Migration changes both ends of the journey: the place people leave and the place they go. Building on push and pull factors, this lesson looks at the effects. Geographers and economists agree on many of them and still debate how large some are.

Remittances are money migrants send home; for some countries they are a large share of national income. Brain drain is the loss of educated, skilled people from a sending country; brain gain is their arrival in a receiving one. Migration also changes the age structure, culture and labor supply of both places.

head: Sending place (origin)
Receiving place (destination)
rows: Remittances; less unemployment; returning migrants bring skills and savings
More workers, often of working age; new businesses; skills; cultural variety
Brain drain; fewer young workers; families separated
Pressure on housing and services in some places; competition for some jobs; adjustment for newcomers and residents
blocks.cap: Effects at both ends.

blocks.html: Migrants are usually young adults, so a place that loses many of them ages faster and loses workers, while a place that gains them gets younger. Migrants earn more where they move, and many send part of their pay home, which can pay for schooling, housing and small businesses. When doctors or engineers leave, a poor country loses people it paid to train; when they send money home or return with experience, it may gain some back.

blocks.title: Naming the effect
blocks.q: Many nurses trained in one country move abroad for higher pay. What effects might each country see?
steps: Sending country: a brain drain of trained nurses, but remittances sent home.
Receiving country: a brain gain that helps fill nursing jobs.
blocks.a: Brain drain plus remittances at home; brain gain abroad.

blocks.title: Reading a pyramid
blocks.q: A rural region's pyramid has unusually short bars for ages 20–39. What is a likely cause?
steps: The missing ages are young working adults.
Young adults are the most likely to migrate, often to cities for work.
blocks.a: Out-migration of young adults.

blocks.html: Students see only one side: "migration helps" or "migration hurts." Researchers find gains and costs for both sending and receiving places, and the balance depends on who moves, where, and under what rules. They still debate how large some effects are, such as the effect on wages of workers already living in a place. Name effects on both sides, and avoid treating one study as the final word.

blocks.html: Geographers use the word culture for the beliefs, practices, languages, foods, clothing, music and ways of building that a group of people shares and passes on. Like the regions you studied, cultures have places where they are found and borders that blur.

A culture trait is one part of a culture, such as a food, a holiday, a style of house or a language. Folk culture is traditional, practiced by a small, often rural group, and passed on by family and neighbors; it changes slowly and varies from place to place. Popular culture spreads widely and quickly through mass media and trade, changes fast, and looks similar in many places.

head: Folk culture
Popular culture
rows: Slowly, person to person, often by relocation
Quickly, through mass media, trade and the internet
blocks.cap: Folk and popular culture compared.

blocks.html: The difference is about how a trait spreads, not how old it is. Folk traditions are learned from family and neighbors, so they stay tied to the places where those people live. Popular culture is carried by television, recorded music, chain stores and the internet, so it can appear in many places at once. That is why a town's main street of chain stores can look much like another town's across the country.

blocks.title: Folk or popular?
blocks.q: Classify: (a) a quilt pattern a family has passed down for generations in one county; (b) a dance that spreads around the world in a month through online videos.
steps: (a) Learned in a family, tied to one place, changing slowly: folk culture.
(b) Spread by media across huge distances at once: popular culture.
blocks.a: (a) folk, (b) popular.

blocks.title: A culture kept on purpose
blocks.q: Old Order Amish communities in Pennsylvania and Ohio travel by horse and buggy and keep many traditional crafts. Folk or popular?
steps: The practices are learned within a small, close-knit community.
They change slowly, by community choice.
They mark the landscape: buggies, farms without power lines.
blocks.a: Folk culture.

blocks.html: Students think folk culture is old and popular culture is new. Age is not the test. A song can be centuries old and still be popular culture if it is spread by mass media, and a new practice can be folk culture if it spreads only by local tradition. Ask: how does it spread, and over how large an area?

blocks.html: You can read culture traits in the land itself. Walk down any street and you see choices people made: what to build, what to plant, what to name things and how to lay out roads.

The cultural landscape is the visible mark people leave on the land: buildings, fields, fences, roads, signs, monuments, places of worship and cemeteries. The geographer Carl Sauer made it a central idea of geography in "The Morphology of Landscape" (1925): culture shapes the natural landscape into a cultural one.

items: Architecture: house styles, roof shapes, building materials.
Land use: field shapes, farm layouts, street grids.
Language in the landscape: street signs, shop signs, place names.
Sacred spaces: churches, mosques, temples, synagogues, shrines, cemeteries.
Sequent occupance: layers left by groups who lived in a place one after another.

blocks.html: People build what their culture values, using the materials and skills they know. So the landscape records culture even when no one is around to ask. A town with signs in two languages, a mosque beside a church and a street grid laid out by surveyors tells a story about who lives there and who lived there before. Reading a landscape is like reading data: it is evidence for how people use a place.

blocks.title: Reading a street
blocks.q: A street in a U.S. city has signs in English and Vietnamese, a pho restaurant, a Buddhist temple and a Catholic church. What does the landscape suggest?
steps: Two languages on signs: many residents or customers speak Vietnamese.
The restaurant and temple show traits carried by migrants.
The church shows another group, or the same group's varied faiths.
blocks.a: A neighborhood shaped by Vietnamese immigrants alongside other groups.

blocks.title: Layers in one place
blocks.q: A New Mexico town has an old adobe church built under Spanish rule, a plaza at its center and newer ranch-style houses. What idea does this show?
steps: Each group that lived there left buildings in its own style.
The layers remain side by side.
blocks.a: Sequent occupance: layers left by successive groups.

blocks.html: Students look only at famous buildings. The cultural landscape is mostly ordinary things: house styles, fences, mailboxes, street names, shop signs and the shapes of fields. These everyday features often tell you more about a culture than one grand monument.

blocks.html: Every culture trait starts somewhere, at a hearth, and spreads, or diffuses, from there. Distance decay explains why nearby places usually adopt a trait first. Geographers name the ways traits spread.

Relocation diffusion: people carry the trait when they move. Expansion diffusion: the trait spreads outward while staying strong at home. It has three kinds: contagious (person to person, to the nearest places first), hierarchical (from big or powerful places to smaller ones, skipping places in between) and stimulus (the underlying idea spreads, but people change the trait to fit their own culture).

blocks.name: gg-diffusion
blocks.cap: Step through each kind of diffusion. Bigger dots are bigger cities.

blocks.html: The kind of diffusion depends on how people come into contact. A joke spreads by contact, so it moves like a ripple. A new fashion often starts in a few large, connected cities, because that is where designers, media and travelers meet, then reaches smaller towns later. When migrants settle far away, the trait jumps with them. And when a trait clashes with local beliefs or tastes, people keep the idea but change the details.

blocks.title: Naming the kind
blocks.q: Classify: (a) English spreading to Australia with British settlers; (b) a fast-food chain in India selling vegetarian burgers instead of beef; (c) a new phone first sold in the largest cities, then in small towns.
steps: (a) Settlers carried the language to a new land: relocation.
(b) The idea (fast-food burgers) spread, but it changed to fit local diets: stimulus.
(c) It moved down from the largest places to smaller ones: hierarchical.
blocks.a: (a) relocation, (b) stimulus, (c) hierarchical.

blocks.title: Contagious diffusion
blocks.q: A rumor in a school moves from one friend group to the next, classroom by classroom. Which kind?
steps: It spreads by direct contact to the nearest people.
Nobody carries it to a distant place, and big places are not skipped to.
blocks.a: Contagious diffusion.

blocks.html: Students call any spread "contagious." Check the path. If a trend jumps from big city to big city before reaching small towns, it is hierarchical. If migrants carry it to a new land, it is relocation. If the idea arrives but is changed to fit local culture, it is stimulus. Contagious diffusion moves outward to the nearest places first, like a ripple.

blocks.html: Language is one of the clearest culture traits, and its spread shows diffusion over thousands of years. Linguists group languages by ancestry, the way a family tree groups cousins.

A language family is a group of languages descended from one ancestor language. The largest family by number of speakers is Indo-European (about 45 percent of the world's people speak one as a first language), then Sino-Tibetan. Other large families include Afro-Asiatic, Niger-Congo, Austronesian and Dravidian.

blocks.name: humangeo-tree
blocks.cap: Some language families, with a few of their languages.

blocks.html: Linguists find families by comparing words and grammar. Families share regular sound patterns in basic words such as numbers, body parts and family members, which are rarely borrowed. Those patterns show common descent. Languages that merely sit side by side borrow words but keep different grammar and basic vocabulary. A few languages, such as Basque in Spain and France, have no known relatives at all: they are called language isolates.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Finnish, Estonian and Hungarian (orange) are Uralic languages; their neighbors mostly speak Indo-European languages.

blocks.title: Neighbors from different families
blocks.q: Hungary is surrounded by countries that speak Indo-European languages. Is Hungarian Indo-European?
steps: Being neighbors does not make languages related.
Hungarian's basic words and grammar match Finnish and Estonian, not German or Slovak.
So it belongs to the Uralic family.
blocks.a: No. Hungarian is Uralic.

blocks.title: Matching languages to families
blocks.q: Which family does each belong to: Swahili, Arabic, Tagalog, Tamil?
steps: Swahili: Niger-Congo (a Bantu language).
Arabic: Afro-Asiatic.
Tagalog (the basis of Filipino): Austronesian.
Tamil: Dravidian.
blocks.a: Niger-Congo, Afro-Asiatic, Austronesian, Dravidian.

blocks.html: Students assume languages in the same country or region belong to the same family. Finnish and Hungarian are Uralic, not Indo-European like most of their neighbors; Basque is related to no other language; India has major Indo-European languages in the north and Dravidian languages in the south. Family is about ancestry, not location.

Where the first Indo-European speakers lived is debated. The two main ideas place them on the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas (the steppe hypothesis) or in Anatolia, spreading with farming (the Anatolian hypothesis). Many scholars now favor the steppe, but research continues.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography: course units and topics

blocks.html: Big language families split into branches, and branches into groups and single languages. Indo-European, the largest family, has about ten branches; four of them have most of its speakers.

blocks.name: humangeo-tree
blocks.cap: Branches of Indo-European, with some of their languages.

blocks.html: Main branches of Indo-European: Germanic (English, German, Dutch, Swedish), Romance (Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian, Romanian; all from Latin), Balto-Slavic (Russian, Polish, Ukrainian, Czech, Lithuanian) and Indo-Iranian (Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi, Persian). Smaller branches include Celtic, Hellenic (Greek), Albanian and Armenian.

A branch forms when speakers of one language spread out and lose touch. Over centuries each group's speech changes in its own way until the groups can no longer understand each other. Latin is the best-documented case: as the Roman Empire's Latin-speaking lands drifted apart after its fall, local Latin became Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian. Branches stay recognizable because their basic words still match: compare English father, German Vater and Dutch vader.

head: English
German
Spanish
Italian
Russian
blocks.cap: Basic words in five Indo-European languages (Russian written in the Latin alphabet). Related words, from one ancestor.

blocks.title: English's branch
blocks.q: A large share of English words (by some counts, more than half of those in a big dictionary) come from French and Latin. Is English a Romance language?
steps: Borrowing words does not change a language's ancestry.
English grew from the speech of Germanic peoples (Angles, Saxons, Jutes) who settled in Britain.
After the Norman Conquest of 1066, English borrowed many French words, but its basic words (I, you, mother, water, house) and grammar stayed Germanic.
blocks.a: No. English is Germanic, with many borrowed Romance words.

blocks.title: Sorting by branch
blocks.q: Which branch: Portuguese, Polish, Persian, Swedish?
steps: Portuguese comes from Latin: Romance.
Polish: Balto-Slavic.
Persian: Indo-Iranian.
Swedish: Germanic.
blocks.a: Romance, Balto-Slavic, Indo-Iranian, Germanic.

blocks.html: Students put English in the Romance branch because so much of its vocabulary is French or Latin. Look at the most basic words and the grammar, which change slowly and are rarely borrowed. Those are Germanic, so English is Germanic. Also, Romance comes from Roman (Latin), not from "romantic."

blocks.html: When people whose languages differ need to trade or work together, they find ways to talk. Over time, these contact languages can turn into something lasting.

A lingua franca is a language used for communication between people with different first languages (English in science and business, Swahili in East Africa). A pidgin is a simplified mix of languages that grows up for contact and has no native speakers. A creole is a pidgin that has become the first language of a community, with a full grammar and vocabulary.

A pidgin starts as a tool: traders or workers take words mostly from one language and use a simple grammar so they can be understood. When children grow up hearing the pidgin as their main language, they expand it into a complete language, with all the grammar any language has. That new language is a creole. Haitian Creole (from French and West African languages) is one of Haiti's two official languages, with French; Tok Pisin (largely from English) is an official language of Papua New Guinea.

head: Kind
Native speakers?
Example
rows: Yes, but used mostly as a second language
Swahili in East Africa; Latin in medieval Europe
blocks.cap: Three kinds of contact language.

blocks.html: The name comes from the original lingua franca, a trade language of Mediterranean ports for centuries, built mostly on Italian with words from other languages.

blocks.title: Pidgin or creole?
blocks.q: On an island, sailors and plantation workers used a simple contact language. Their grandchildren speak it at home as their first language. What is it now?
steps: It began as a contact language with no native speakers: a pidgin.
Children learned it as a first language, so it gained native speakers and a full grammar.
blocks.a: A creole.

blocks.title: A lingua franca
blocks.q: A Brazilian engineer and a Japanese engineer write their shared report in English. What role is English playing?
steps: Neither speaks English as a first language.
They use it to communicate across languages.
blocks.a: A lingua franca.

blocks.html: Students treat pidgins and creoles as "broken" versions of other languages. A creole is a full language, with its own regular grammar, learned by children as their first language and used for everything from songs to law. A pidgin is simpler because it is a contact tool, not because its speakers lack skill.

blocks.html: Religion shapes calendars, foods, laws, landscapes and where people live. Geographers do not judge beliefs; they study where religions are found and how they spread. One of their main tools is a simple two-way grouping.

Universalizing religions aim to appeal to all people everywhere and often seek converts: Christianity, Islam, Buddhism and Sikhism. Ethnic religions are closely tied to one people, culture and homeland, and grow mainly through birth into the community: Hinduism, Judaism and Shinto are common examples.

head: Universalizing
Ethnic
rows: Open to anyone; many seek converts
Mostly by birth into a people
Wide, by missionaries, trade and empires (expansion and relocation)
Mostly stays in its homeland; spreads when its people migrate (relocation)
Usually a founder and a known starting point
blocks.cap: How the two kinds differ geographically.

blocks.html: The grouping explains a pattern on the map. A religion that invites everyone tends to spread far beyond its hearth. A religion tied to one people's land, history and customs tends to stay concentrated where that people lives, and appears elsewhere mainly where its members have migrated. The grouping describes how religions spread, not their size, age or value.

blocks.title: Size is not the test
blocks.q: Hinduism has about 1.2 billion followers (2020). Why is it called an ethnic religion?
steps: The test is how it is tied to a people and a place, not its size.
Most Hindus live in India and Nepal, and the religion is closely tied to the land, rivers and traditions of South Asia.
It has spread abroad mainly as Indian families migrated.
blocks.a: It is closely tied to one people and region, and spreads mainly by migration.

blocks.title: Reading a map pattern
blocks.q: A religion is found in many unconnected regions on several continents. Which kind is it more likely to be?
steps: A wide, scattered pattern suggests spread by missionaries, trade or conversion.
blocks.a: Universalizing.

blocks.html: Students judge a religion as universalizing by its size. Hinduism has over a billion followers but is an ethnic religion, because it is closely tied to one people and region. Smaller religions can be universalizing. Also remember that real religions are more varied than any two-way grouping; some ethnic religions accept converts, for example. Use the grouping as geographers do: to explain patterns of spread.

blocks.html: Every religion has a hearth, the place where it began. Most of the world's largest religions began in two regions of Asia. From there, the kinds of diffusion you have studied carried them across the world, as the universalizing and ethnic grouping predicts.

head: Religion
Hearth
How it spread
rows: Mainly relocation, as Jewish communities lived in many lands (the diaspora)
Missionaries along Roman roads; made the Roman Empire's official religion in AD 380; later carried to the Americas, Africa and Asia
Southwest Asia (Mecca, Arabian Peninsula), 7th century AD
Expanding states and empires across North Africa and Asia; traders across the Indian Ocean to Southeast Asia
