blocks.html: Religions travel the way other culture traits do: with people. Where traders, armies, pilgrims and missionaries traveled, beliefs went too. A religion that welcomed converts could spread by expansion diffusion along trade routes and through empires, while religions tied to one people spread mostly by relocation, when their people moved. That is why the map of religions today follows old routes such as the Silk Road and the Indian Ocean sea lanes.

Judaism, Christianity and Islam began in Southwest Asia; Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism began in South Asia. They spread by trade, migration, missionaries and empires, so a religion can end up strongest far from its hearth.

blocks.title: Far from the hearth
blocks.q: Buddhism began in South Asia. Where do most Buddhists live today, and why?
steps: Missionaries and traders carried Buddhism east along the Silk Road and sea routes.
It took root in China, Korea, Japan and much of Southeast Asia.
In India its share of the population declined over many centuries.
China alone has about half of the world's Buddhists.
blocks.a: In East and Southeast Asia, where it spread by expansion diffusion.

blocks.title: Trade routes
blocks.q: The country with the most Muslims today is Indonesia, far from Arabia. How did Islam get there?
steps: Muslim merchants sailed Indian Ocean trade routes.
Coastal trading towns in Southeast Asia adopted Islam through contact with them.
It spread inland over centuries.
blocks.a: By traders along Indian Ocean sea routes.

blocks.html: Students assume a religion is strongest where it began. Buddhism began in India, but most Buddhists today live in East and Southeast Asia. Christianity began in Southwest Asia, but most Christians live in the Americas, Europe and Africa. Follow the paths of diffusion, not just the hearth.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography: course units and topics

blocks.html: When people meet through migration, trade or conquest, cultures change. Diffusion explains how traits travel; this lesson names what happens when they arrive.

Acculturation: a group adopts some traits of another culture while keeping its own (learning a new language for work but speaking the home language with family). Assimilation: a group takes on the larger culture so fully that its original culture fades. Syncretism: two cultures blend into something new. Multiculturalism: several cultures live side by side, each keeping its identity.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: Immigrants learn the national language for work but cook and pray as at home
Grandchildren of immigrants speak only the new language and keep no old customs
A holiday that mixes Indigenous traditions with Catholic feast days
A music style that fuses two traditions into a new sound
A family adds the new country's holidays to its own

blocks.cap: Sort the examples.

blocks.html: Change happens in degrees. Newcomers usually adopt the traits they need first: language for work and school, sometimes clothing and food. Whether the home culture survives depends on how large and close-knit the group is, whether it keeps ties with the homeland, and how the larger society treats it. Across several generations, many immigrant families in the United States have shifted to English, a classic path toward assimilation; others keep their language for generations.

blocks.title: Day of the Dead
blocks.q: Mexico's Day of the Dead combines older Mesoamerican customs of honoring ancestors with the Catholic feasts of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day. Which process is this?
steps: Traits from two cultures combined.
The result is a new, distinct tradition, not one culture replacing the other.
blocks.a: Syncretism.

blocks.title: Three generations
blocks.q: A grandmother speaks only her home language. Her son speaks both languages. His daughter understands only the new country's language and celebrates only its holidays. Describe the change.
steps: The son shows acculturation: he added the new language and kept the old one.
The granddaughter shows assimilation: the original culture has largely faded.
blocks.a: Acculturation in the second generation, assimilation by the third.

blocks.html: Students treat acculturation and assimilation as the same. With acculturation, people keep their own culture while adding new traits; with assimilation, the original culture fades away. And syncretism is neither: it creates something new from both. Ask: is the old culture still there, gone, or blended?

blocks.html: Globalization is the growing connection of places through trade, travel, media and the internet. Thanks to time-space compression, popular culture can now reach most of the world within days. What does that do to cultures when they meet?

Globalization spreads popular culture worldwide, which can push out local traditions (cultural convergence: places becoming more alike). It also brings local foods, music and languages to the world, and leads many communities to protect and revive their traditions (cultural divergence). Glocalization is when global products and ideas are adapted to local cultures.

Global chains, films, music and social media make the same products and trends available almost everywhere, so landscapes and habits can grow more alike. But the flow runs in many directions: foods, music and games from many countries have become popular worldwide. And seeing one's own culture threatened can make people value it more. Hawaiian-language preschools and schools, for example, have raised a new generation of speakers since the 1980s. Scholars debate how much globalization makes cultures alike and how much it mixes and renews them.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: The same coffee chain on main streets in many countries
A community opens schools taught in its traditional language
A global restaurant chain adds local dishes to its menu in each country
A local craft festival revived to attract visitors and young people
Teenagers in many countries following the same online trends

blocks.cap: Sort the examples.

blocks.title: Glocalization
blocks.q: A worldwide fast-food chain sells vegetarian burgers in India and rice dishes in parts of Asia. Which idea is this?
steps: The global brand spread.
It changed its products to fit local tastes and beliefs.
blocks.a: Glocalization (the same idea as stimulus diffusion).

blocks.title: Two directions
blocks.q: Give one example of globalization making places more alike and one of it spreading a local culture outward.
steps: More alike: the same chain stores, films and phone apps in cities around the world.
Spreading outward: a regional food, such as sushi from Japan, now eaten worldwide.
blocks.a: Chain stores (convergence); sushi spreading worldwide (a local trait going global).

blocks.html: Students think globalization simply makes all places the same. It does spread popular culture, but it also carries local foods, music and languages to the world, and many places revive or protect their traditions in response. Look for change in both directions, and treat "how much" as a question scholars still debate.

blocks.html: In everyday American speech, a "state" is Ohio or Texas, and "nation" and "country" mean the same thing. Political geographers use these words more carefully, because the difference explains many of the world's borders and many of its tensions. You met the idea of shared culture in culture traits, and the world's count of countries in World Geography.

A state is a political unit: a territory with a permanent population, a government and borders, that runs its own affairs (a country). A nation is a people who share a culture and see themselves as one group. A nation-state is a state whose people are mostly one nation.

The two ideas come from different places. A state is a legal fact: the Montevideo Convention of 1933 lists four tests, a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other states. A nation is a feeling of belonging, built from a shared language, history, religion or customs. Because borders were often drawn by rulers, wars and treaties rather than by the people living there, the two do not always line up.

blocks.title: Is Japan a nation-state?
blocks.q: Japan is a sovereign country, and most of its people share the Japanese language and a sense of common history. Is it a state, a nation or a nation-state?
steps: Japan has a government, borders and a permanent population, and it deals with other countries: it is a state.
Most people in Japan see themselves as one people, the Japanese: that is a nation.
The state and the nation largely match.
Smaller groups, such as the Ainu and the Ryukyuan peoples, also live there, so it is close to, not perfectly, a nation-state.
blocks.a: Close to a nation-state: one state whose people are mostly one nation.

blocks.title: The word "state" in two senses
blocks.q: A news story says "the state of Ohio" and a geography book says "the state of Brazil." Do they mean the same thing?
steps: Ohio is one of the 50 parts of the United States. It shares power with the national government and does not deal with foreign countries on its own.
Brazil is a sovereign country, a member of the United Nations.
In political geography, only Brazil is a state; Ohio is a state in the U.S. sense, a part of a federal country.
blocks.a: No. Brazil is a sovereign state; Ohio is a unit inside one.

blocks.html: Reading "state" as a U.S. state and "nation" as a country. In this unit, a state is a sovereign country and a nation is a people. A nation can live in one state, be split across several, or have no state at all, as the next topic shows.

By the count used across this course, there are 195 countries: the 193 members of the United Nations and the 2 observer states, the Holy See and the State of Palestine. A few other places, such as Taiwan and Kosovo, govern themselves and are recognized by some countries but not by others; Sovereignty explains why.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: A nation-state is the textbook ideal, but it is rare. Most states hold several nations, and many nations spill across borders. Geographers have names for each way the two can fail to match.

A multinational state contains two or more nations (the United Kingdom, Belgium, Russia). A multistate nation is one nation living in two or more states (Koreans in North and South Korea). A stateless nation has no state of its own (the Kurds).

head: Pattern
Meaning
Examples
rows: The United Kingdom (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland); Belgium (Flemish and Walloons); Switzerland (four national languages); Russia, India and Nigeria (many peoples)
Koreans in North Korea and South Korea; Hungarian communities in Hungary and its neighbors
The Kurds; the Basques of Spain and France; the Roma of Europe

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Kurds' homeland in the mountains where Türkiye, Iraq, Iran and Syria meet. No state is named for the Kurds; Iraq has a self-governing Kurdistan Region.

blocks.html: Borders were drawn by empires, wars and treaties, often long before anyone asked which people lived where. When the Ottoman Empire broke up after World War I, the new borders divided the Kurds' homeland among several states. Today an estimated 30 to 40 million Kurds live mostly in Türkiye, Iraq, Iran and Syria, which makes them one of the largest nations without a state. Estimates vary because several of these countries do not count people by ethnic group.

blocks.title: Classify Belgium
blocks.q: Belgium has Dutch-speaking Flemish people in the north and French-speaking Walloons in the south, under one national government. Which pattern is it?
steps: Count the states: one, Belgium.
Count the nations: at least two, the Flemish and the Walloons.
One state with several nations is a multinational state.
blocks.a: A multinational state.

blocks.title: Classify the Koreans
blocks.q: Most Koreans share a language and history, but since 1948 they have lived in two states, North Korea and South Korea. Which pattern is it?
steps: Count the nations: one, the Koreans.
Count the states: two.
One nation in two or more states is a multistate nation.
blocks.a: A multistate nation.

blocks.html: Assuming most countries are nation-states. Few states are made of a single nation; most hold several peoples, and many people live in a state named for a different group. Ask two questions every time: how many states? and how many nations?
A people can belong to more than one level at once: a person can feel Scottish and British, or Catalan and Spanish. Geographers describe these identities; they do not rank them.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: A state is more than a patch of land with a government. What makes it a state is that no outside power rules it. That right has a name.
Sovereignty is a state's right to govern its own territory and people without outside control. Territoriality is the way people and states claim, mark and defend space as their own.

The modern idea of sovereignty is often traced to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended decades of war in Europe and set the principle that each ruler governs inside their own borders. Sovereignty has two sides. Inside, the government makes and enforces the laws. Outside, other states accept that it is in charge there, which is called recognition. A place can have the first without the second, and that is where hard cases appear.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Disputed areas are hatched. Tap one, such as Taiwan, Kosovo, Western Sahara or Somaliland, to read how it is governed and who claims it.

blocks.html: Some places govern themselves but are recognized by only some countries. Taiwan is governed by the Republic of China, with its capital at Taipei; the People's Republic of China claims it, and only a small number of countries recognize the Republic of China, while many others keep unofficial ties. Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008; more than 100 UN members have recognized it, while Serbia and many others have not. This course describes such places and the claims about them; it does not decide them.

items: Territoriality in daily life: fences, "Private property" signs, gang or team turf, a towel on a beach chair.
Territoriality of states: border posts, flags, maps, passports and patrols.
Sharing instead: Antarctica has no countries; under the Antarctic Treaty (1959), seven countries' claims are set aside and the continent is used for peace and science.

blocks.title: Two sides of sovereignty
blocks.q: A government collects taxes, runs schools and controls its borders, but most countries do not formally recognize it as a state. Which side of sovereignty does it have?
steps: Running its own affairs at home is the inside side.
Being accepted by other states is the outside side, recognition.
It has the first and only partly the second.
blocks.a: It governs itself (internal sovereignty) but lacks wide recognition, so its status is disputed.

blocks.title: Territoriality or not?
blocks.q: Which shows territoriality: (a) a country placing markers along its border, (b) two countries agreeing to study a shared river together?
steps: Territoriality means claiming and marking space as one's own.
Border markers announce "this side is ours."
Joint study is cooperation, not a claim.
blocks.a: (a), the border markers.

blocks.html: Thinking every place that governs itself is fully sovereign. Recognition by other states matters too. Places like Taiwan and Kosovo run their own affairs but are recognized by some countries and not others, so their status is described as disputed, with each side's claim stated plainly.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Every sovereign state needs a line where its authority stops. Geographers sort these boundaries two ways: by what the line follows, and by when it was drawn compared with settlement.

By what they follow, boundaries are physical (a river, mountain range or lake), cultural (a language or religion line) or geometric (a straight line of latitude or longitude). By when they were drawn, they are antecedent (before most settlement), subsequent (after settlement, as the land filled in), superimposed (forced on an area by outsiders) or relict (no longer working, but still visible).

Meaning
Example
rows: The Rio Grande (U.S. and Mexico); the Pyrenees (France and Spain); the Andes (Chile and Argentina)
Follows a language, religion or ethnic line
Many borders in Europe roughly follow language areas
A straight line, often a parallel or meridian
The 49th parallel between the U.S. and Canada; many lines across the Sahara
Drawn before most of today's settlement
The 49th parallel, set by treaties in 1818 and 1846
Drawn after settlement, as groups settled their limits
Many European borders, fixed and refixed over centuries
Much of Africa, divided by European powers after the Berlin Conference (1884-1885)
No longer a boundary, still seen on the land
The former border between East and West Germany (1949-1990); the Great Wall of China

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Africa's political map. Look for the long straight segments across the Sahara: lines drawn on maps by outside powers.

blocks.html: Why so many straight lines in Africa and the American West? A straight line is easy to draw on a map and to describe in a treaty ("along the 49th parallel"), even by people who have never seen the land. In Africa, European powers at and after the Berlin Conference divided the continent with little regard for the peoples living there; some peoples, such as the Somali, ended up split among several states.

blocks.title: Two labels for one border
blocks.q: The U.S.-Canada border west of the Great Lakes runs along the 49th parallel, agreed in 1818 and 1846, when few settlers of either country lived there. Name its type by shape and by timing.
steps: Shape: it is a straight line of latitude, so it is geometric.
Timing: it was drawn before most of today's settlement, so it is antecedent.
blocks.a: Geometric and antecedent.

blocks.title: A wall that is no longer a border
blocks.q: East and West Germany reunited in 1990. Traces of the old border remain as a strip of land, museums and a line still visible in some statistics. What type of boundary is it now?
steps: It no longer divides two states.
But you can still see it on the land and in the data.
That is a relict boundary.
blocks.a: A relict boundary.

blocks.html: Thinking straight borders are natural. Straight lines usually mark borders drawn on maps by outsiders or by treaty, as in much of Africa and the western United States. Natural borders follow rivers and mountain crests, and they wiggle.

blocks.html: A boundary is an agreement, and agreements can be read differently. Geographers sort boundary disputes by what the two sides disagree about, not by how heated the dispute is.

Definitional: over the wording of the treaty that defines the border. Locational: over where the line falls on the ground. Operational: over how the border works (crossings, trade, migration). Allocational: over resources the border divides (oil, water, fish, minerals).

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: Two countries read the treaty phrase "the main channel of the river" differently
A river shifts course in a flood, and land ends up on the other bank
Neighbors disagree about opening a crossing for trucks
An oil field lies under the border
Two countries both want to fish in waters near the line
Old maps from two surveys put the line in different places

blocks.cap: Sort each dispute by what it is about.

blocks.html: The four kinds often come in a chain. Vague treaty words (definitional) can leave the line's position unclear (locational). And a border that is fixed on the ground can still cause arguments about how it works (operational) or what lies under it (allocational). Naming the kind of dispute helps people see what would settle it: a new survey, a reworded treaty, a crossing agreement, or a plan to share a resource.

blocks.title: The Chamizal
blocks.q: The Rio Grande forms part of the U.S.-Mexico border. A flood in 1864 moved the river south, and about 600 acres near El Paso and Ciudad Juárez ended up north of the new channel. Both countries claimed the land until they settled it in the Chamizal Convention of 1963. What kind of dispute was it?
steps: The treaty said the border follows the river. Nobody disputed that wording.
The question was where the line falls now that the river had moved.
A dispute about where the line lies on the ground is locational.
blocks.a: Locational (settled by the 1963 Chamizal Convention).

blocks.title: A lake between two countries
blocks.q: Two neighbors agree exactly where their border crosses a lake, but argue over how much water each may take from it. What kind of dispute is it?
steps: The line itself is agreed, so it is not definitional or locational.
The argument is about sharing a resource the border divides.
That makes it allocational.
blocks.a: Allocational.

blocks.html: Sorting a dispute by how serious it is. Sort it by what it is about: the words of a treaty, the line's place on the ground, crossing rules, or resources such as oil or water. A quiet disagreement about fishing is allocational; so is a tense one.

Many disputes in the world today are described in this course only by the claims each side makes. In practice problems you will sort made-up cases, so the skill is the classification, not taking a side.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Land boundaries stop at the shore, but countries also need rules at sea: who may fish, drill and sail where. Since 1982 most countries follow one treaty.

Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, adopted 1982), distances are measured from the coast's baseline in nautical miles (1 nautical mile = 1,852 meters). The territorial sea runs to 12 nautical miles; the contiguous zone to 24; the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) to 200. Beyond that are the high seas, open to all.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: The zones of the sea, from the coast outward (not to scale).

head: Zone
Distance from the baseline
What the coastal country controls
rows: Nearly everything, as on land; foreign ships still have the right of innocent passage
Enforcement of customs, immigration, tax and health laws
Rights to fish, oil, gas and other resources; other countries may sail and fly through
No single country; open to all

blocks.html: The rules balance two needs. Coastal countries want their nearby fish and seabed minerals, and the means to stop smuggling. Every country needs ships to move freely, since most world trade goes by sea. So control is strongest near the shore and weakens step by step: full sovereignty, then enforcement, then resources only.

blocks.title: Which zone?
blocks.q: A foreign fishing boat is 150 nautical miles off a country's coast. May it fish there without permission? May a foreign cargo ship sail through?
steps: 150 is more than 24 and less than 200, so the spot is in the exclusive economic zone.
The EEZ gives the coastal country the rights to its fish, so the boat needs permission to fish.
Ships of every country may sail through an EEZ.
blocks.a: No to fishing without permission; yes to sailing through.

blocks.title: When zones overlap
blocks.q: Two countries face each other across a sea 300 nautical miles wide. How far can each EEZ reach?
steps: Each could claim 200 nautical miles, but 200 + 200 = 400, more than 300.
The zones overlap, so the two countries must agree on a dividing line; a common choice is the line halfway between the coasts.
Halfway: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 nautical miles each.
blocks.a: About 150 nautical miles each, if they use the halfway (median) line.

blocks.html: Thinking a country owns the sea out to 200 nautical miles. Beyond 12 nautical miles, ships of every country may pass; the EEZ gives rights to resources, not full control. And in the territorial sea itself, foreign ships may pass peacefully.

Most countries are parties to UNCLOS. The United States signed an agreement on its seabed mining part in 1994 but has not ratified the treaty; it follows most of the treaty's navigation and zone rules in practice. Where a continental shelf extends far from shore, a country may claim seabed rights beyond 200 nautical miles, up to set limits.

blocks.html: Look at a country's outline and you learn something about how easy it is to govern, defend and connect. Geographers name five common shapes. They are tools for describing, not rules that decide a country's fate. You drew on outlines like these in Kinds of Boundaries.

Compact: roughly round, the capital near the middle (Poland). Elongated: long and thin (Chile). Prorupted: compact with a long arm sticking out (Thailand). Perforated: surrounds another country (South Africa around Lesotho). Fragmented: in separate pieces (Indonesia).

blocks.name: gg-outline
blocks.cap: Four shapes: Poland (compact), Chile (elongated), Thailand (prorupted) and South Africa, with Lesotho as a hole inside it (perforated).

blocks.name: gg-outline
blocks.cap: Indonesia: a fragmented state of thousands of islands.

head: Shape
Possible advantage
Possible challenge
More examples
rows: Short distances; easy to connect from the center
Varied climates and resources along its length
Far ends hard to reach and connect
The arm can reach a river, the sea or a resource
The arm can be hard to reach from the core
Namibia (the Caprivi Strip), Afghanistan (the Wakhan Corridor)
The surrounding state controls routes in and out
Depends on good relations with the country inside
Italy (around San Marino and Vatican City)
Pieces separated by water or other countries
The Philippines, Malaysia; the U.S. with Alaska and Hawaii

blocks.html: Shape matters because distance matters. In a compact state, roads and services can reach every place from the capital quickly. In an elongated or fragmented state, the far parts are far away, which can make them harder to serve and can feed a sense of being left out. Shape is only one factor: rich, well-connected countries of every shape do well.

blocks.title: Name the shape
blocks.q: A country is one solid piece, but a narrow strip of its land runs far out from the main body to reach a river. Which shape is it?
steps: It is one piece, so it is not fragmented.
Its main body is compact, but it has an arm sticking out.
A compact body with an arm is prorupted.
blocks.a: Prorupted, like Namibia with the Caprivi Strip reaching toward the Zambezi River.

blocks.title: Perforated or fragmented?
blocks.q: Italy completely surrounds San Marino and Vatican City. Is Italy perforated or fragmented?
steps: Fragmented means the country itself is in separate pieces.
Perforated means it has a hole: another country inside it.
Italy surrounds two other countries, so it has holes.
blocks.a: Perforated. (Italy also has islands, Sicily and Sardinia, so it is partly fragmented too: a country can show more than one shape.)

blocks.html: Mixing up perforated and fragmented. A perforated state surrounds another state, like a doughnut around its hole; a fragmented state is in several separate pieces. The country inside a perforated state is often landlocked and enclaved, like Lesotho.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Every sovereign state has to decide how power is spread between the national government and the regions. There are two main designs. You may know the U.S. version from Federalism Basics in the Civics course.

In a unitary state, power is concentrated in the central government; regions carry out its decisions and have only the powers it gives them (France, Japan). In a federal state, the constitution divides power between the national government and states or provinces, and each level has authority of its own (the United States, India, Germany).

head: Unitary
Federal
rows: Divided by the constitution between national and regional governments
Can the center change the regions' powers by itself?
Usually no; it takes a constitutional change
Smaller or more culturally uniform states
Large states, or states with distinct regional peoples
The United States, Canada, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, India, Australia, Nigeria

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Some unitary and federal states. Federal systems are common among very large countries.

blocks.html: Why choose federalism? It lets a large country, or one with very different regions, keep national unity while letting regions run schools, police and roads in their own way. Canada's provinces let French-speaking Québec keep its own civil law, for example. Why choose a unitary system? It can make laws the same everywhere and decisions faster. Both designs work; each has trade-offs.

Many unitary states have handed some power to regions, a process called devolution. The United Kingdom stays a unitary state, but since the late 1990s Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have had their own elected bodies. Forces That Unite and Divide explores why.

blocks.title: Which design?
blocks.q: In Country X, the national parliament can abolish a province's council by passing an ordinary law. Is X unitary or federal?
steps: Ask whether regional power is protected by the constitution.
Here the center can take it away by ordinary law.
So regional power is on loan from the center.
blocks.a: Unitary.

blocks.title: A federal check
blocks.q: In the United States, can Congress abolish the state of Ohio's legislature by passing a law?
steps: The U.S. Constitution guarantees the states and reserves powers to them.
Changing that would take a constitutional amendment, not an ordinary law.
blocks.a: No. That is the mark of a federal state.

blocks.html: Thinking a federal state has a weak center. Federal systems divide powers by law; both levels have real authority. The U.S. national government runs the military, money and foreign policy, while states run much of education and policing.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Every state, unitary or federal, has things that hold it together and things that strain it. Geographers borrow two words from physics for them.

Centripetal forces pull a state together: a shared language or religion, national symbols, a respected government, good transportation, a common outside threat. Centrifugal forces pull it apart: regional differences in language, religion or wealth, poor connections, and a sense of unfair treatment. Strong centrifugal forces can lead to devolution, the transfer of power from the center to regions.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: A national holiday that everyone celebrates
A highway and rail network linking every region
A region whose people speak a different language and feel ignored
A national team in the World Cup
A wealthy region that feels it pays for the rest
A remote region with no road to the capital

blocks.cap: Sort each force.

blocks.html: A difference by itself does not divide a state. Switzerland has four national languages and is stable. A difference becomes centrifugal when it lines up with a region (a group concentrated in one area), and with a grievance (a feeling of unfair treatment). Then people may ask for more self-government. States often respond with devolution: Spain's 1978 constitution opened the way for its autonomous communities, and in 1999 the United Kingdom opened a Scottish Parliament and a Welsh assembly.

items: Ethnic and cultural forces: language, religion, a separate history.
Economic forces: a region much richer or poorer than the rest.
Spatial forces: distance and barriers, such as islands far from the capital or mountains between regions.

blocks.title: Sort a force
blocks.q: A country's capital is on the mainland, and an island region 1,000 km away gets few ferries and little investment. Is the distance centripetal or centrifugal?
steps: Distance and poor links make it harder to feel part of the whole.
Add the sense of being neglected, and the region has a grievance.
blocks.a: Centrifugal (a spatial force with an economic grievance).

blocks.title: When is a difference not divisive?
blocks.q: A country has two languages, spoken all over the country rather than in separate regions, and both are official. Is this likely to be a strong centrifugal force?
steps: A difference divides most when it matches a region and a grievance.
Here the speakers are mixed together, and both languages are respected.
blocks.a: Probably not; with no separate region and no grievance, it is a weak dividing force.

blocks.html: Treating any difference as centrifugal. A difference becomes a dividing force when it lines up with a region and a sense of grievance. Many diverse countries are stable, and some fairly uniform ones have regional tensions over money or distance.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: States are sovereign, but they also join groups to trade, defend each other or solve shared problems. Such groups sit "above" the state.

A supranational organization links three or more states that agree to cooperate, sharing some decisions. Examples: the United Nations (1945), the European Union, NATO (1949, a defense alliance), the African Union (2002, following the Organization of African Unity of 1963) and ASEAN (1967, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations).

head: Organization
Main purpose
How binding?
rows: Peace, security, cooperation on health, food, refugees and more
Most decisions are recommendations; Security Council decisions can bind members
A single market, shared laws, free movement; many members share the euro
Very: EU law applies in every member
Mutual defense: an attack on one is treated as an attack on all
Cooperation, peace and development across Africa
Trade and cooperation in Southeast Asia
Works by consensus; looser than the EU

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The 27 members of the European Union, highlighted.

blocks.html: Why give up any control? Small and medium states gain bargaining power, bigger markets and shared security by acting together. A business in one EU country can sell in all 27 under one set of rules. The cost is that some decisions are made jointly rather than at home, and people in member states debate how much should be shared. Geographers describe that debate and the trade-offs on each side.

blocks.title: Supranational or not?
blocks.q: Which is a supranational organization: (a) a city council, (b) a trade agreement among eight countries with a shared secretariat, (c) a national army?
steps: Supranational means above the state: several states joined together.
A city council is below the state; a national army belongs to one state.
blocks.a: (b), the eight-country trade group.

blocks.title: Matching purpose
blocks.q: A group of countries promises that an attack on any one of them will be treated as an attack on all. What kind of organization is this, and what is a real example?
steps: The promise is about defense, not trade.
A mutual-defense alliance in Europe and North America, founded in 1949, is NATO.
blocks.a: A military alliance; NATO.

blocks.html: Thinking joining means giving up all sovereignty. Members share some decisions; how much varies, from the EU's common laws to looser groups that work by agreement. Members remain states: they keep their own governments, and they can leave.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Boundaries are drawn inside countries too. In the United States, the 435 seats in the House of Representatives are divided among the states after each census (reapportionment), and then each state draws its districts (redistricting). The Civics course covers the rules in Apportionment and Redistricting; here we look at the geography.

Gerrymandering is drawing district lines to give one group an advantage. Two techniques: packing (putting many of the other side's voters into a few districts, so they win those by huge margins and waste votes) and cracking (spreading the other side's voters thinly across many districts, so they fall short in each).

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Packing: group A has 60% of the voters, but packed into two districts it wins only 2 of 5.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Cracking: the same voters, with B's voters spread across all five districts. A wins all 5 and B wins none.

blocks.html: With winner-take-all districts, it is not just how many votes a group has, but where its voters are counted. A vote beyond what is needed to win a district, or a vote in a district the group loses, does not add a seat. Whoever draws the lines can arrange those wasted votes. The word comes from 1812, when a Massachusetts district signed into law by Governor Elbridge Gerry was said to look like a salamander.

blocks.title: Count the seats
blocks.q: Five districts of 100 voters each. Group A has 260 of the 500 voters, arranged as 90, 90, 30, 25, 25 in the five districts. How many districts does A win?
steps: A wins a district with more than 50 of its 100 voters.
Districts with 90 and 90: A wins both. Districts with 30, 25, 25: A loses all three.
blocks.a: A wins 2 of 5 districts with 52% of the votes: A's voters were packed.

blocks.title: Is an odd shape proof?
blocks.q: A district has a long, twisting shape. Is it gerrymandered?
steps: Districts must have nearly equal populations and often follow rivers, county lines, coastlines and communities.
Any of these can make a strange shape.
The question is the effect on representation, which needs the vote numbers, not just the outline.
blocks.a: Not necessarily. Shape alone does not prove it.

blocks.html: Thinking odd shapes always mean gerrymandering. Districts also follow rivers, county lines and equal-population rules; the test is the effect on representation, which courts and voters judge under the law. A neat, compact map can also favor one side.

People disagree about who should draw district lines. Some states let the legislature draw them; others use independent or bipartisan commissions. Supporters of legislatures say elected officials answer to voters; supporters of commissions say mapmakers should not draw their own districts. This course describes both views.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: For most of human history, people lived by hunting, fishing and gathering wild plants. Then, in several parts of the world, people began to plant seeds and tend animals. Farming is a great example of the diffusion you have studied: it began in a few hearths and spread.

Farming began about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago, starting in the Fertile Crescent of Southwest Asia, and arose independently in several hearths: China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea, Africa's Sahel and eastern North America. Each hearth domesticated its own plants and animals.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Hearths of farming. Each began with local wild plants and animals.

head: Hearth
About when
Early crops and animals
rows: Wheat, barley, lentils; sheep, goats, cattle
Millet in the north, rice in the south; pigs
Sunflower, squash and other seed plants
blocks.cap: Dates are rounded; archaeologists keep refining them.

blocks.html: How do we know the hearths were independent? The crops differ. Wheat came from wild grasses of Southwest Asia, maize from a wild Mexican grass called teosinte, and the potato from wild Andean plants. None of these wild plants grew in the other hearths, so each farming system had to begin where its wild ancestors lived. Afterward, crops spread far: wheat to Europe, maize to the whole world after 1492.

blocks.title: Match a crop to its hearth
blocks.q: Archaeologists find early domesticated potatoes. In which hearth were they most likely grown?
steps: Potatoes came from wild relatives in the highlands of South America.
That is the Andes hearth (today's Peru and Bolivia).
blocks.a: The Andes.

blocks.title: One hearth or many?
blocks.q: Maize was being farmed in Mexico thousands of years before anyone in the Americas could have learned of wheat farming in Southwest Asia. What does that tell us?
steps: There was no contact across the oceans then.
Farming in Mesoamerica used a local plant, teosinte, turned into maize.
So it began there on its own.
blocks.a: Farming arose independently in more than one hearth.

blocks.html: Thinking farming was invented once and spread from one place. It began separately in several regions, each with its own crops and animals. Diffusion came later, as crops and ideas spread out from each hearth.

blocks.html: Farming did not stay the same after the first hearths. Three great changes, called agricultural revolutions, each let fewer farmers feed more people.

The First Agricultural Revolution was the start of farming itself, about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago. The Second, beginning in Britain in the 1700s, brought new crop rotations, new tools and, later, machines and fertilizers. The Green Revolution (1940s-1970s) spread high-yield seeds, chemical fertilizer and irrigation in Asia and Latin America.

head: Revolution
When and where
What changed
What followed
rows: From about 10,000 BC, in several hearths
Britain from the 1700s, then Europe and North America
The Norfolk four-course rotation (wheat, turnips, barley, clover); Jethro Tull's seed drill (1701); enclosure of fields; selective breeding; later tractors and fertilizers
Food for growing industrial cities; fewer farm workers
1940s-1970s, Mexico, India, Pakistan, the Philippines and more
High-yield wheat and rice (such as the rice IR8, 1966), more fertilizer, more irrigation
Much larger harvests; debates about cost and environment

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: Wild wheat becomes a planted crop
Turnips and clover replace fallow fields in a rotation
A short-stemmed, high-yield rice variety
Horse-drawn seed drill plants in rows
Taming sheep and goats
Wheat bred in Mexico, planted across India and Pakistan

blocks.cap: Sort each change into its revolution.

blocks.html: Each revolution raised the food grown per worker or per acre. Clover adds nitrogen to soil, so the Norfolk rotation removed the need to leave fields empty (fallow). Short-stemmed Green Revolution wheat and rice could take more fertilizer without falling over, so yields rose. More food per farmer freed people for other work, which helped industry and cities grow. That link ties this topic to The Spread of Industry.

blocks.title: Why short stems?
blocks.q: Green Revolution wheat and rice were bred to be shorter. Why did that matter?
steps: Fertilizer makes plants grow heavy heads of grain.
Tall plants with heavy heads fall over (lodge), and the grain is lost.
Short, sturdy stems hold the heavy heads up.
blocks.a: They could use more fertilizer and carry bigger harvests without falling over.

blocks.title: Put them in order
blocks.q: Order these: high-yield rice IR8; the seed drill; the first planted barley.
steps: First planted barley: the First Agricultural Revolution, about 10,000 BC.
The seed drill: 1701, the Second.
IR8 rice: 1966, the Green Revolution.
blocks.a: Barley, seed drill, IR8.

blocks.html: Thinking the Green Revolution meant organic farming. It meant new high-yield varieties with more fertilizer and water; it raised harvests and also raised debates about cost and environment. Supporters point to the famines it helped avoid; critics point to water use, fertilizer runoff and costs for small farmers. Both sets of facts are part of the record.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Farmers decide how much work, money and materials to put into each acre. That choice sorts farming into two broad kinds, whatever the crop. The agricultural revolutions gave farmers new ways to add those inputs.

Intensive farming puts a lot of labor or capital (machines, fertilizer, water, buildings) on each unit of land, and gets a large output from a small area: market gardens, rice paddies, dairies, feedlots. Extensive farming uses large areas with little input per acre: ranching, nomadic herding, shifting cultivation.

head: Intensive
Extensive
blocks.cap: Measure inputs per acre or per hectare, not the size of the farm.

blocks.html: Why farm intensively? Where land is expensive or scarce, every acre must produce a lot, so farmers add labor and capital. Near cities, land costs more (the idea behind the von Thünen model), and in crowded river valleys of Asia, families make small plots very productive. Where land is cheap and plentiful, as in dry grasslands, it pays to use a lot of it lightly.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: A family hand-weeds and floods a one-hectare rice paddy
Cattle graze 20,000 hectares of dry range
A heated greenhouse grows tomatoes year-round
Herders move goats and camels with the seasons
A dairy with milking machines near a city
A forest plot is cleared, farmed two years, then left to regrow

blocks.cap: Sort each farm by input per unit of land.

blocks.title: Compare per hectare
blocks.q: Farm A: 2 hectares, 3,000 hours of work a year. Farm B: 500 hectares, 6,000 hours a year. Which is more labor-intensive?
steps: Farm A: 3,000 ÷ 2 = 1,500 hours per hectare.
Farm B: 6,000 ÷ 500 = 12 hours per hectare.
Farm B uses more hours in total, but far fewer per hectare.
blocks.a: Farm A, with 1,500 hours per hectare.

blocks.title: Big and modern, but extensive?
blocks.q: A wheat farm on the Great Plains covers 2,000 hectares with two workers and big machines. Is it intensive or extensive?
steps: The machines are capital, but spread over 2,000 hectares, the input per hectare is small.
Output per hectare is modest compared with a market garden.
blocks.a: Extensive, even though it is large and modern.

blocks.html: Thinking intensive means large and modern. Intensive is about input per unit of land: a small, hand-worked rice paddy is intensive; a vast cattle ranch is extensive. Always divide by the land.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: The second question about any farm is who eats what it grows. This cuts across the intensive and extensive split, so every farm gets two labels.
Subsistence farmers grow food mainly to feed their own families, selling little. Commercial farmers grow crops and raise animals to sell, often to distant markets.

head: Intensive
Extensive
rows: Intensive subsistence: wet rice in East and South Asia
Shifting cultivation in tropical forests; pastoral nomadism in dry lands
blocks.cap: Two questions, four boxes.

blocks.html: Subsistence farming is common where incomes are low, roads to markets are few, and families need a sure food supply. Commercial farming grows with roads, cities and trade, and it often becomes agribusiness: farming linked with companies that supply seed and machines and that process, ship and sell the food. Commercial farms often grow one crop on a large scale (monoculture), which is efficient but can raise risks from pests and price swings.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: A family in the Andes grows potatoes to eat through the winter
A Brazilian farm ships soybeans overseas
Herders in the Sahel live on their animals' milk and meat
An Iowa farm sells corn to an ethanol plant
A plantation exports bananas
A village clears a forest plot to grow its own cassava

blocks.cap: Who eats the harvest?

blocks.title: Two labels
blocks.q: A family in Bangladesh grows rice on one hectare, working long days and eating most of the harvest. Label it twice.
steps: Who eats it? The family: subsistence.
Input per hectare? Very high labor on a small plot: intensive.
blocks.a: Intensive subsistence farming.

blocks.title: Shifting cultivation
blocks.q: A farmer in a rainforest clears and burns a small plot, grows crops for the family for two or three years, then moves on and lets the forest regrow. Label it twice.
steps: The family eats the crops: subsistence.
A plot is used for a short time, then rests for many years, so the land per family is large and inputs per hectare are low: extensive.
blocks.a: Extensive subsistence farming (shifting cultivation, also called slash-and-burn or swidden).

blocks.html: Thinking subsistence farming is always extensive. Shifting cultivation and herding are extensive, but intensive rice farming in Asia is often subsistence too. Answer the two questions separately.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: A world map of farming looks a lot like a map of climate zones. Climate and soil set what can grow; markets and transportation decide what pays.

Plantations grow in the tropics; Mediterranean farms grow grapes, olives and citrus; dairy farms sit near cities in cool, wet regions; grain grows on wide plains; ranchers and nomadic herders use dry lands; shifting cultivation is found in tropical rainforests.

head: Farming type
Climate
Where, for example
rows: Plantation (coffee, cocoa, bananas, sugarcane, palm oil)
Central America, West Africa, Southeast Asia, Brazil
Dry, hot summers; mild, rainy winters
Around the Mediterranean Sea, California, central Chile
Northeastern U.S., Wisconsin, northwestern Europe, New Zealand
U.S. Great Plains, Canadian Prairies, Ukraine, Argentina's Pampas
Mixed crop and livestock (corn, soybeans, hogs)
The U.S. Corn Belt, much of Europe
The Sahel, Arabia, Central Asia, Mongolia
Amazon Basin, Central Africa, parts of Southeast Asia

blocks.name: gg-climate

titles: Tropical rainforest: shifting cultivation and plantations

blocks.cap: Two climates, two farming systems. Grapes and olives handle the dry summer; tropical crops need heat and rain all year.

blocks.html: Plants have needs: a growing season long enough, enough rain at the right time, and no killing frost for tropical crops. Olive trees survive the Mediterranean's dry summers that would ruin corn. Cocoa needs warmth and rain all year. Within what climate allows, money decides: milk spoils, so dairies cluster near cities; dry grain keeps and ships well, so it can grow far from buyers.

blocks.title: Read the climate
blocks.q: A region has dry, hot summers and mild, rainy winters. Which farming fits best: plantation bananas, Mediterranean grapes and olives, or commercial dairy?
steps: Dry summers and rainy winters are the Mediterranean climate.
Grapes and olives are adapted to summer drought.
Bananas need rain and warmth all year; dairy needs green pasture.
blocks.a: Mediterranean grapes and olives.

blocks.title: Why near the city?
blocks.q: Two farms have the same climate. One is 20 km from a big city; the other is 800 km away. Which is more likely to be a dairy farm?
steps: Fresh milk spoils fast and is heavy to ship.
The farm close to the city can get it to buyers quickly and cheaply.
blocks.a: The farm 20 km from the city.

blocks.html: Thinking any crop can grow anywhere with enough work. Climate and soil set what grows best; markets and transport decide what pays. Greenhouses can grow tomatoes in winter, but at a cost that only pays near rich markets.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: In 1826 a German landowner, Johann Heinrich von Thünen, asked a simple question: if every acre were the same, what would farmers grow at each distance from the market? His answer, in The Isolated State, explains the farming patterns around cities in his day and shows how geographers use models.

Imagine one market town on a flat, uniform plain, with no roads and the same soil everywhere. Because carrying goods costs more the farther they go, farm uses form rings: market gardening and dairy closest, then forest (wood for fuel and building), then grains and field crops, and ranching farthest out.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: The von Thünen model: rings of land use around one market town.

blocks.html: Each farmer earns what is left after paying to grow the crop and to haul it: a profit, or land rent, per hectare. Near town every use is profitable, so land goes to the use that earns the most there: perishable, heavy or bulky goods such as milk, vegetables and firewood, which cost a lot to haul. Farther out, those costs eat their profit, and uses that are cheap to move per hectare, such as grain and animals that walk to market, win instead.
The idea can be written as a formula, with yield $Y$ (tons per hectare), price $p$ and growing cost $c$ (per ton), freight rate $f$ (per ton per km) and distance $d$ (km):
$$\text{rent per hectare} = Y(p - c) - Y f d$$

blocks.title: Rent at a distance
blocks.q: Wheat yields 3 tons per hectare, sells for 200 and costs 120 per ton to grow, and hauling costs 1 per ton per km. What is the rent per hectare at 30 km?
steps: Profit before hauling: $3 \times (200 - 120) = 240$.
Hauling: $3 \times 1 \times 30 = 90$.
blocks.a: 150 per hectare.

blocks.title: Where the ring ends
blocks.q: For the same wheat, how far from market does the rent fall to zero?
steps: Set $Y(p - c) = Y f d$, so $d = (p - c) / f$.
Beyond 80 km, growing wheat for this market loses money.
blocks.a: 80 km.

blocks.html: Thinking the rings come from soil. In the model the land is the same everywhere; the rings come from the cost of carrying goods to market. Real maps add rivers, roads, refrigeration and different soils, which stretch and break the rings, but the logic of transport cost still shows up.

Von Thünen put forest in the second ring because wood for fuel and building was heavy and needed in large amounts. That ring has faded from modern maps since coal, oil and trucks changed the costs, a reminder that a model fits the conditions it was built for.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Fly over farm country and you see two patterns: where people live, and how the land is divided. Both come from history and culture as much as from the land, and both connect to the kinds of farming you have met.

Rural settlements are clustered (homes grouped in a village, fields around it), dispersed (farmhouses spread out, each on its own land) or linear (homes strung along a road, river or canal). Land is divided by metes and bounds (natural features and distances), the township-and-range grid, or long lots (narrow strips running back from a river).

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Three ways to divide land: metes and bounds, township and range, and long lots.

head: Survey system
How it works
Where in North America
rows: Boundaries follow natural features and measured distances: "from the oak tree to the creek…"
The original thirteen colonies and lands settled from them
Township and range (the Public Land Survey System)
A grid of townships 6 miles square, each split into 36 sections of 1 square mile (640 acres)
Most land west of the Appalachians, starting with Ohio
Narrow lots fronting a river, running far back from it
French settlements along the St. Lawrence River and in Louisiana

blocks.html: Each system fit a moment. Early colonists marked land by what they could see. After independence, the Land Ordinance of 1785 had the new government survey its western lands into squares before selling them, so plots could be described and sold quickly. French settlers gave each family a strip of riverbank, because the river was the road. You can still see these patterns from the air: square fields in Iowa, irregular ones in Virginia, ribbon fields in Québec.

blocks.title: Count the acres
blocks.q: A township has 36 sections. How many acres is a quarter section, and how many acres is the whole township?
steps: One section is 1 square mile = 640 acres.
A quarter section: 640 ÷ 4 = 160 acres.
A township: 36 × 640 = 23,040 acres.
blocks.a: 160 acres; 23,040 acres.

blocks.title: Read the landscape
blocks.q: In an area, farmhouses sit far apart, each on its own square farm, along roads that meet at right angles every mile. Name the settlement pattern and the survey system.
steps: Houses far apart, each on its own farm: dispersed.
Square farms and roads every mile: the township-and-range grid.
blocks.a: Dispersed settlement on a township-and-range survey.

blocks.html: Thinking square farm fields are natural. Township-and-range squares come from the U.S. Land Ordinance of 1785; older Eastern lands follow metes and bounds, and French areas long lots. The land did not make the squares; a law did.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Since the Green Revolution, the world grows more food than ever, and people argue about how it should be grown, who grows it and who can get it. Geographers lay out the evidence and the trade-offs. On many of these questions, the facts point in different directions, and values decide how people weigh them.

Four common debates: genetically modified (GM) crops, organic farming, large versus small farms, and food access (food deserts). Learn what each side argues and what the evidence shows; do not expect one side to win every point.

head: Debate
Arguments made for
Arguments made against or concerns
rows: Higher yields, less insecticide on some crops, crops that resist drought or pests; major science reviews (such as the U.S. National Academies, 2016) found approved GM foods no riskier to eat than conventional ones
Weeds and insects that evolve resistance, seed patents and the power of a few companies, effects on neighboring farms; many consumers want labels
No synthetic pesticides or fertilizers, attention to soil health
Yields average roughly 20% lower, so more land is needed for the same food; prices are higher
Lower cost per unit of food; feeds cities cheaply
Fewer farm jobs, less variety, effects on rural towns
Higher cost per unit; "food miles" are only part of food's environmental cost

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: Organic yields average lower than conventional yields
Lower food prices matter more than farm jobs
A census tract is more than 1 mile from a supermarket
Every food with GM ingredients should carry a label
Herbicide-resistant weeds have spread in some regions
Small family farms are a better way of life

blocks.cap: Separate checkable facts from value judgments.

blocks.html: Debates last when they mix facts with values. A study can measure yields, prices or pesticide use. It cannot tell you how much to care about cheap food versus rural jobs, or about choice versus convenience. That is why careful people end up on different sides.

Food deserts. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has described a food desert as a low-income census tract where at least 500 people, or a third of the people, live more than 1 mile (in cities) or 10 miles (in rural areas) from a supermarket. People debate the remedies: new stores, transit, delivery, or programs that change what people buy.

blocks.title: Apply the definition
blocks.q: A low-income urban tract of 4,000 people has 1,600 living more than 1 mile from a supermarket. Does it meet the food-desert test?
steps: The test: at least 500 people or at least one third live beyond 1 mile (urban).
1,600 is more than 500, and 1,600 ÷ 4,000 = 40%, more than a third.
blocks.a: Yes, on both counts.

blocks.title: Fact or value?
blocks.q: Sort: (a) "Organic farms used no synthetic fertilizer." (b) "Organic food is worth the higher price."
steps: (a) can be checked against the farm's records.
(b) depends on what a person values and can afford.
blocks.a: (a) is a checkable fact; (b) is a value judgment.

blocks.html: Expecting one side to be right on every question. On many food questions, scientific findings, costs and values point in different directions; know what each side argues, and which claims are facts that evidence can settle.

blocks.html: In Population Distribution you saw where people live. One of the biggest changes of the last two centuries is where within a country they live: more and more of them in cities. World Geography's largest cities topic shows the giants.

Urbanization is the growth in the share of a population living in urban areas. By countries' own definitions, about 30% of the world's people were urban in 1950 and about 55% in 2018, and the UN projected about 68% by 2050 (World Urbanization Prospects 2018). Urbanization is fastest today in Africa and Asia.

Cities grow three ways: people move in from the countryside (rural-to-urban migration, pulled by jobs and services and pushed by too little farmland), people are born there (natural increase), and villages at the edge grow until they are counted as part of the city (reclassification). The first agricultural revolutions and industry made this possible: when fewer farmers can feed everyone, most people can work in cities.

head: Urban share
Note
rows: The same source; countries' own definitions of "urban"
Most of the growth in Asia and Africa

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The three largest urban areas in the UN's World Urbanization Prospects 2025, which measured cities in a new way.

blocks.html: Ways of counting change the answer. The UN's 2025 report used a new, uniform method (the "Degree of Urbanisation"), which counts a city as all the continuous dense settlement around it. By that method, Jakarta (nearly 42 million), Dhaka (almost 40 million) and Tokyo (about 33 million) were the largest in 2025. Older lists, built from each country's own boundaries, put Tokyo first. When you compare city sizes, check the source and the year.

blocks.title: Compute the urban share
blocks.q: A country has 40 million people, and 26 million live in urban areas. What percent is urban?
steps: Urban share = urban population ÷ total population.

blocks.title: Size or share?
blocks.q: Country A's cities grew from 5 to 6 million people while its total grew from 10 to 15 million. Did A urbanize?
steps: Before: $5 \div 10 = 50\%$ urban.
After: $6 \div 15 = 40\%$ urban.
The cities got bigger, but the share fell.
blocks.a: No. Its urban share fell from 50% to 40%, even though cities grew.

blocks.html: Thinking the largest cities are in rich countries. Most of today's largest and fastest-growing cities are in Asia and Africa. Many rich countries are already highly urbanized, so their urban share changes slowly.

blocks.html: You met site and situation as two ways to describe any place. They also explain why cities grow where they do, and why some keep growing while others fade.

A city's site is the land it stands on: a harbor, a river crossing, an island, a hill that is easy to defend, a spring. Its situation is its location relative to other places: on a trade route, at a crossroads, near resources and markets.

head: City
Site
Situation
rows: An island in the Seine (the Île de la Cité), easy to defend and to cross
Center of a rich farming region and of France's roads and railroads
The Erie Canal (1825) linked it to the Great Lakes and the Midwest
A small island with a good harbor
On the Strait of Malacca, one of the world's busiest shipping routes
Flat, marshy land by Lake Michigan
Where water routes and, later, railroads met, linking East and West
Hills by a natural harbor (the Golden Horn)
Where Europe meets Asia and the Black Sea meets the Mediterranean

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Singapore sits at the southern end of the Strait of Malacca, between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.

blocks.html: A good site gets a settlement started: people needed water, defense and a place to land boats. But a site does not change while the world around it does. When trade routes, canals, railroads or airports shift, a city's situation can improve or decline. That is why situation often matters more over time, and why cities spread far beyond their first site.

blocks.title: Site or situation?
blocks.q: Which describes Singapore's situation: (a) it is on a small island with a sheltered harbor; (b) it lies on the main shipping route between the Indian and Pacific oceans?
steps: Site is the land itself: the island and the harbor.
Situation is the location relative to other places: the shipping route.
blocks.a: (b) is its situation.

blocks.title: A canal changes everything
blocks.q: In 1825 the Erie Canal connected the Hudson River with the Great Lakes. Did it change New York City's site or its situation?
steps: The land under the city did not change.
Its connection to the interior did: farm goods from the Midwest could now ship out through its harbor.
blocks.a: Its situation, which helped it grow into the largest U.S. city.

blocks.html: Thinking a city stays important because of its first site. Many cities grew past their first reason for being; situation often matters more over time. A defensive hill means little today, but a port on a busy route or a hub airport means a lot.

blocks.html: Why do small towns have a gas station and a grocery but no sports arena? In 1933 the German geographer Walter Christaller offered an answer in his study of towns in southern Germany. It builds on the distance decay you met earlier: people go farther for some things than for others.

A central place is a town that provides goods and services to the area around it (its market area, or hinterland). Each good has a threshold, the minimum number of customers needed to stay in business, and a range, the farthest distance people will travel to buy it.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Christaller's pattern: hexagonal market areas, with a few large central places and many small ones.

head: Low-order goods
High-order goods
rows: A heart surgeon, a pro sports team, a major airport
Small: a few hundred to a few thousand people
Large: hundreds of thousands or millions
Short: people will not drive far for gas

blocks.html: A good is offered only if enough customers live within its range to meet its threshold. Groceries pass that test almost everywhere, so they are in every village. A specialty hospital needs so many patients that only a big city has enough people within reach. The result is a hierarchy: many hamlets and villages with low-order goods, fewer towns, and a few cities that offer everything. Christaller drew market areas as hexagons because hexagons cover a plain with no gaps and no overlaps, the way circles cannot.

blocks.title: Does the store open?
blocks.q: A bookstore needs 6,000 customers (its threshold). People will travel 5 km for it (its range). The area around the town has 80 people per square km. Is the threshold met?
steps: The market area is a circle of radius 5 km: $\pi \times 5^2 \approx 78.5$ square km.
People inside: $78.5 \times 80 \approx 6{,}280$.
6,280 is more than 6,000.
blocks.a: Yes, barely: about 6,280 people live within range.

blocks.title: Threshold or range?
blocks.q: A new movie theater closes because, although people come from 30 km away, there are not enough of them. Was the problem the range or the threshold?
steps: The range (30 km) was large.
The number of customers was too small.
blocks.a: The threshold was not met.

blocks.html: Mixing up threshold and range. Threshold is how many customers are needed; range is how far a customer will go. A memory hook: threshold counts totals of people, range is road distance.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 6: Cities and Urban Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Line up a country's cities from largest to smallest. Is there a pattern in their sizes? In many countries there is, and its exceptions tell a story too. This builds on central place theory and uses division as in fractions as division.

The rank-size rule says the city of rank $n$ has about $1/n$ the population of the largest city: the 2nd largest about half, the 3rd about a third, and so on. A primate city is more than twice as large as the next largest city, and dominates its country.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: The rank-size rule: city 2 is half of city 1, city 3 is a third, and so on.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: A country with a primate city: one giant, then much smaller cities.

blocks.html: The rule is an observed pattern (related to a broader one called Zipf's law), not a law of nature. It shows up where a large country has a full hierarchy of central places. A primate city usually reflects history: the capital of a once-centralized kingdom or a colony, where government, trade, ports and universities all gathered in one place. The geographer Mark Jefferson named the pattern in 1939; his examples included Paris and Bangkok.

blocks.title: Predict a city
blocks.q: The largest city in a country has 6,000,000 people. If the rank-size rule holds, about how many live in the 4th largest city?
steps: Rank 4 should have about $1/4$ of the largest city.

blocks.title: Primate or not?
blocks.q: Country X's largest city has 8 million people and its second has 1.5 million. Is the largest a primate city?
steps: Primate means more than twice the second city.
Twice the second: $2 \times 1.5 = 3$ million.
8 million is far more than 3 million.
blocks.a: Yes. It is more than five times the second city.

blocks.html: Thinking every country follows the rank-size rule. Countries with a primate city, such as the United Kingdom (London) or Thailand (Bangkok), break it. Small countries and countries with a long history of one central capital often have primate cities.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 6: Cities and Urban Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Inside a city, land uses form patterns: offices downtown, factories by rail lines, rich and poor neighborhoods in different places. Three classic models describe North American cities of the early and middle 1900s. They follow from central place thinking and from bid-rent: land near the center costs the most, so uses that can pay the most locate there.

The concentric zone model (Ernest Burgess, 1925) shows rings around the central business district (CBD). The sector model (Homer Hoyt, 1939) shows wedges along transportation lines. The multiple nuclei model (Chauncy Harris and Edward Ullman, 1945) shows several centers, such as an airport, a university or a suburban business district.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Burgess: rings outward from the CBD, based on Chicago.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Hoyt: wedges along roads, railways and rivers.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Harris and Ullman: several nodes, each pulling related uses near it.

blocks.html: Each model captures something real. Burgess saw new immigrants arriving in the older, crowded zone next to downtown and families moving outward as they could afford it. Hoyt saw that a high-income area, once started along a scenic avenue, keeps growing outward in the same direction, while industry follows the rail lines. Harris and Ullman saw that cars and trucks let cities grow several centers. Later geographers added edge cities (Joel Garreau, 1991): big office and shopping centers at highway interchanges far from downtown.

blocks.title: Which model?
blocks.q: A city's wealthy neighborhoods form a long wedge from downtown along a lakeshore drive, and factories line the railroad on the other side. Which model fits best?
steps: Rings would put each group all the way around the center.
Here each group stretches outward in one direction, along a route.
blocks.a: The sector model.

blocks.title: Many centers
blocks.q: A metropolitan area has its old downtown, a separate office cluster by the airport, and a university district with shops and housing around it. Which model fits best?
steps: There is more than one center, each with related uses around it.
blocks.a: The multiple nuclei model.

blocks.html: Thinking a model describes one real city exactly. Models are simplified patterns; each fits some cities and parts of cities better than others. A real city can show rings near the center, wedges along its rail lines, and several nuclei at its edge.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 6: Cities and Urban Land-Use Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: The North American models assume that the wealthy move outward. In many cities elsewhere, the pattern is different, shaped by colonial history, by where jobs and services are, and by rapid growth. Geographers built models for these regions too.

The Latin American city model (Ernst Griffin and Larry Ford, 1980) has a CBD with a wealthy spine along a grand boulevard, rings that get poorer outward, and peripheral squatter settlements at the edge. Models of sub-Saharan African cities (Harm de Blij) show several CBDs: colonial, traditional and market. Models of Southeast Asian port cities (T. G. McGee, 1967) center on the old port, with commercial, government and market-garden zones around it.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: The Latin American city model.

head: Model
Distinctive features
rows: Elite spine and sector with the best services; zone of maturity; zone of in situ accretion (homes improved bit by bit); peripheral squatter settlements; sometimes "disamenity" zones of very poor housing near the center
Three CBDs (a colonial one, a traditional one and an open-air market); ethnic and mixed neighborhoods; mining and manufacturing zones; informal settlements at the edge
The old colonial port as the focus; Western and "alien" (often Chinese) commercial zones; a government zone; new suburbs, industrial parks and market gardens at the edge

blocks.html: Where cities grew fast and the government could not build housing and roads quickly enough, newcomers built their own homes on open land at the edge, often hillsides or flood plains. Meanwhile, the colonial-era center kept the best services, so the wealthy stayed near it. That reverses the U.S. pattern, where cars and highways let wealthy families move outward. Many squatter settlements grow into established neighborhoods as residents add rooms, water and electricity over the years; that is the "in situ accretion" in the model's name.

blocks.title: Where do the poorest live?
blocks.q: In the Latin American city model, where are the newest and poorest settlements found?
steps: The elite spine runs out from the center.
Rings get less established outward.
At the outer edge are peripheral squatter settlements.
blocks.a: At the edge of the city.

blocks.title: Compare two models
blocks.q: In a North American city, many high-income families live in outer suburbs. In the Latin American model, where do they live?
steps: The Latin American model puts the elite sector next to the CBD, along the spine.
They live near the center, on the main boulevard.
blocks.a: Near the center, along the elite spine.

blocks.html: Applying the U.S. pattern everywhere. In many Latin American cities the wealthy live near the center along a main boulevard, and the poorest live at the edges. Read each city with the model built for its region, and remember that every model simplifies.

blocks.html: Growing cities bring jobs and services together, and also problems of space, cost and fairness. Here are the main challenges and the main responses, each with debated effects. They build on the models of cities you have studied.

Common challenges: sprawl (low-density growth spreading outward), traffic, housing costs, informal settlements and segregation. Common responses: public transit, new urbanism (walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods), smart growth (steering growth into existing areas, sometimes with urban growth boundaries), and redevelopment.

head: Response
What supporters say
What critics say
rows: Urban growth boundary (Portland, Oregon, since the 1970s)
Protects farmland, encourages transit and infill
Limits land for building, which can raise housing prices
Walkable streets, shops near homes, less driving
Can be costly; some projects become high-priced enclaves
Moves many people in little space; helps those without cars
Expensive to build; works best at high density

cards.text: Houses spreading over farmland far from jobs
A light-rail line with homes and shops around its stations
Rents rising faster than wages
A neighborhood designed so shops and schools are a short walk away
Homes built without permits on a hillside at the city's edge
A line around the city beyond which new subdivisions are limited

blocks.cap: Challenge or response?

blocks.html: Many responses trade one good against another. Limiting sprawl protects farmland and shortens commutes, but limiting land can raise prices. New investment improves a neighborhood, and higher property values help owners but can push renters out. That is why the same policy draws praise and criticism.

Gentrification is the arrival of higher-income residents and investment in an older, lower-income neighborhood. The word was coined in 1964 by the sociologist Ruth Glass, describing London. Worldwide, about 1.1 billion people lived in slums or informal settlements in 2022 (UN-Habitat estimate), mostly in fast-growing cities of Africa and Asia.

blocks.title: Name the trade-off
blocks.q: A city draws a growth boundary to protect farms. What is one benefit and one cost people point to?
steps: Benefit: farmland and open space are protected, and development is steered closer to existing roads and transit.
Cost: less land for new homes can push housing prices up.
blocks.a: It protects farmland but may raise housing costs.

blocks.title: Two views of one change
blocks.q: Old warehouses become apartments and cafés. Rents in the area rise 40% in five years. Describe it from two points of view.
steps: A homeowner or a new business may welcome rising values, new shops and safer streets.
A long-time renter may be unable to afford to stay.
blocks.a: Gentrification: investment and new services, and displacement pressure on renters.

blocks.html: Thinking gentrification is simply good or bad. It can bring investment and also raise rents for long-time residents; people disagree about how to weigh the two. Describe both effects and who feels each.

blocks.html: Every job adds value somewhere in a chain that runs from the ground to the customer. Geographers sort that work into sectors, and the mix of sectors in a place tells a lot about its economy, as the regions you have mapped show.

The primary sector takes resources from the earth (farming, fishing, forestry, mining). The secondary sector makes things (manufacturing, construction, processing). The tertiary sector provides services (stores, transport, health care, teaching). Some geographers add the quaternary sector (information and research) and the quinary sector (the highest-level decision makers).

head: Sector
What the work is
Examples
rows: Wheat farmer, fisher, logger, copper miner
Steelworker, car assembler, builder, baker in a factory
Cashier, truck driver, nurse, teacher, waiter
Software developer, research scientist, financial analyst
Chief executives, senior government officials, heads of major institutions
