cards.text: A miner digging coal
A worker on a car assembly line
A dentist
An engineer designing a new battery in a lab
A shrimp fisher

blocks.cap: Sort each job by the work itself.

blocks.html: As countries develop, their workers shift from primary to secondary to tertiary work. Machines let fewer farmers grow more food, factories hire the people who leave farms, and, as incomes rise, people spend more on services such as health care, travel and education. Today most workers in rich countries are in the tertiary sector, while in many low-income countries most still work in farming. Economists Allan Fisher and Colin Clark described this shift in the 1930s and 1940s.

blocks.title: Same company, different sectors
blocks.q: A car company employs assembly-line workers, accountants and designers. Which sector does each belong to?
steps: Assembly-line workers make the cars: secondary.
Accountants provide a service: tertiary.
Designers create new designs and information: quaternary.
blocks.a: Secondary, tertiary and quaternary.

blocks.title: Read a workforce
blocks.q: In Country A, 60% of workers farm, 15% work in industry and 25% in services. In Country B, 2% farm, 20% work in industry and 78% in services. Which is more developed, by this measure?
steps: Development usually shifts workers out of farming and into services.
B has very few farmers and most workers in services.
blocks.a: Country B.

blocks.html: Putting a factory's office workers in the secondary sector. Sort by the work itself: designing and managing are services, even inside a manufacturing company. Only the people who make the product are doing secondary-sector work.

blocks.html: For most of history, almost everything was made by hand or with water and animal power. Then, in one corner of Europe, machines and new sources of energy changed how goods were made, and the change spread around the world, much as the diffusion of any innovation does.

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s, with textile machines, coal, iron and James Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1769). It spread to Belgium, France, Germany and the United States in the 1800s, to Japan and Russia late in the 1800s, and after 1950 to East Asia and beyond. Since about 2010, China has had the world's largest manufacturing output.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Industry began in Britain (orange) and spread first to Belgium, France, Germany, the United States and Japan (blue).

blocks.name: gg-diffusion
blocks.cap: Industry often spread hierarchically: to large cities and ports first, then to smaller places.

blocks.html: Why Britain? It had coal and iron close together, a large trading network and empire, capital to invest, a growing population, and inventors and investors rewarded for new machines. Industry then spread where its ingredients could be gathered: coal fields (the Ruhr in Germany, Pennsylvania), ports and, later, cheap labor and good transport. In the late 1900s many factories moved to countries with lower wages, while older industrial regions, such as the U.S. "Rust Belt," lost factory jobs (deindustrialization).

head: Wave
When
Where
rows: Belgium, France, Germany, the United States
South Korea, Singapore, Hong Kong and Taiwan; then China, from about 1980; then Southeast Asia, India, Mexico and others

blocks.title: Order the spread
blocks.q: Put these in the order industry arrived on a large scale: China, Britain, Japan, Germany.
steps: Britain first, from about 1760.
Germany in the 1800s.
Japan in the late 1800s.
China mainly after its reforms beginning about 1980.
blocks.a: Britain, Germany, Japan, China.

blocks.title: Why leave?
blocks.q: A clothing factory moves from the United States to a country where wages are much lower. Which factor changed its best location?
steps: Sewing clothes takes a lot of labor.
Shipping costs per shirt are small.
So labor cost matters most, and it is lower abroad.
blocks.a: Labor cost.

blocks.html: Thinking industry is now leaving the world. Manufacturing has moved around the world; today it is largest in China. In rich countries, factory output often stays high while factory jobs fall, because machines do more of the work.

sources.name: College Board, AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description, Unit 7: Industrial and Economic Development Patterns and Processes

blocks.html: Where should a factory go? In 1909 the German economist Alfred Weber, in Theory of the Location of Industries, argued that firms choose the place where their total costs are lowest. Like von Thünen, he started from transport costs.

Least cost theory: a factory locates where transport, labor and agglomeration costs are lowest. Transport matters most. In a bulk-reducing (weight-losing) industry, the product weighs less than its inputs, so the factory locates near the raw materials. In a bulk-gaining (weight-gaining) industry, the product weighs more than its inputs, so the factory locates near the market.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Bulk-reducing: the least-cost site is pulled toward the raw materials.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Bulk-gaining: the least-cost site is pulled toward the market.

blocks.html: Shipping costs depend on weight times distance. If 100 tons of copper ore make 2 tons of copper, it is far cheaper to smelt near the mine and ship 2 tons than to ship 100 tons of rock. A soft-drink bottler adds heavy water, which is available almost everywhere, to small amounts of syrup, so it ships light syrup and bottles near its customers. Weber added two more pulls: cheap labor can be worth a longer haul, and agglomeration (firms clustering to share workers, suppliers and ideas) can lower costs too.

blocks.title: Near the mine or near the market?
blocks.q: A sawmill turns logs into lumber, losing bark, sawdust and scraps. Where should it locate?
steps: The product (lumber) weighs less than the input (logs).
That makes it bulk-reducing.
Ship the lighter product the long way: build near the forest.
blocks.a: Near the forest (the raw material).

blocks.title: Compare two sites
blocks.q: A plant uses 50 tons of ore to make 10 tons of product. Site A is at the mine, 200 km from the market. Site B is at the market, 200 km from the mine. Shipping costs 1 per ton per km. Which site is cheaper?
steps: Site A ships the product: $10 \times 200 \times 1 = 2{,}000$.
Site B ships the ore: $50 \times 200 \times 1 = 10{,}000$.
Site A costs less.
blocks.a: Site A, at the mine (2,000 versus 10,000).

blocks.html: Mixing up bulk-reducing and bulk-gaining. If the product weighs less than its inputs (copper ore to copper), build near the mine; if it weighs more (bottling soda), build near customers. Ask: "Which end of the trip carries less weight?" Ship that.

Weber's model was built for heavy industry and costly transport. Today, cheap container shipping, just-in-time delivery and the value of skilled workers change the balance, but the weight logic still explains many smelters, sawmills and bottling plants.

blocks.html: Development means improving people's lives: income, health, education and freedom to choose. To compare places, geographers use numbers, and each number shows some things and hides others. The mix of sectors is one clue; here are the main measures. Economics covers GDP itself in what GDP leaves out.

GDP per capita (output per person) and GNI per capita (income per person, including income from abroad) measure money. The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UN Development Programme since 1990, combines three things: a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living. The Gender Inequality Index (since 2010) measures gaps between women and men in health, empowerment and work.

head: Dimension
Indicator
Goalposts (minimum, maximum)
rows: Mean years of schooling (adults 25+) and expected years of schooling (children)
GNI per capita (in purchasing-power dollars), on a log scale
blocks.cap: How the HDI is built (UNDP technical notes).

blocks.html: Each dimension becomes an index from 0 to 1: $(\text{actual} - \text{min}) / (\text{max} - \text{min})$. The education index averages its two parts. The HDI is the geometric mean of the three: $\text{HDI} = \sqrt[3]{I_{\text{health}} \times I_{\text{education}} \times I_{\text{income}}}$. Countries are grouped as very high (0.800 and up), high (0.700 to 0.799), medium (0.550 to 0.699) and low (below 0.550).

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: GDP per capita
GNI per capita
Human Development Index
Gender Inequality Index
Life expectancy
Literacy rate

blocks.cap: Which measures look beyond income?

blocks.html: Why not just use income? Two countries with the same income per person can differ a lot: one may spend on schools and clinics, while in the other a few people hold most of the wealth. The HDI adds health and schooling so those differences show. The geometric mean means a country cannot make up for very poor health with very high income: a low score in any one dimension pulls the whole index down.

blocks.title: Compute an HDI
blocks.q: A country's health index is 0.80, its education index 0.60 and its income index 0.70. What is its HDI, and which group is it in?
steps: Multiply: $0.80 \times 0.60 \times 0.70 = 0.336$.
Take the cube root: $\sqrt[3]{0.336} \approx 0.695$.
blocks.a: About 0.695: medium human development.

blocks.title: The health index
blocks.q: Life expectancy is 72 years. What is the health index?
steps: Use the goalposts 20 and 85.

blocks.html: Treating GDP per capita as a full measure of well-being. It leaves out health, education and how income is shared, which is why the HDI adds them. And remember that every index is an average: it can hide large differences between regions or groups inside a country.

blocks.html: Why are some countries rich and others poor, and how do countries develop? Scholars have answered in very different ways. You can measure development; theories try to explain it. Learn each one and its critics; none is settled fact.

Rostow's stages of growth (1960) say every country can climb the same five stages, from traditional society to high mass consumption. Wallerstein's world-systems theory (1974) sees one world economy with a core, a semi-periphery and a periphery, linked by trade. Dependency theory (Raúl Prebisch and others, from the 1950s) argues that poorer countries were kept poor by unequal ties to richer ones.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: Rostow's five stages of economic growth.

blocks.name: gg-models
blocks.cap: World-systems theory: core, semi-periphery and periphery.

head: Theory
Main idea
What critics say
rows: Five stages: traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, high mass consumption. Investment, trade and new technology move a country up.
Assumes one path modeled on Western countries; underplays history, colonialism and global power
Core countries do high-skill, high-wage work; the periphery supplies raw materials and cheap labor; the semi-periphery has some of each. Countries can move between tiers.
Can underplay a country's own choices and institutions; tiers are hard to define
Exporting raw materials and importing manufactured goods keeps poorer countries dependent; ties to rich countries can hold them back.
Countries that traded heavily, such as South Korea, grew rich; some policies based on it, like high tariffs, had mixed results

blocks.html: The theories look at different scales. Rostow looks inside each country, at savings and investment. World-systems and dependency theory look at the whole world economy, at who makes what and who trades with whom. Real cases support parts of each, which is why geographers learn all three and many say countries have developed by different paths.

blocks.title: Which theory is speaking?
blocks.q: A writer argues that a country stays poor because it exports coffee and copper and imports machinery, and the prices of its exports fall relative to its imports. Which theory?
steps: The argument is about unequal trade ties, not stages inside the country.
Falling relative prices of raw-material exports were a central point for Prebisch.
blocks.a: Dependency theory.

blocks.title: Place a stage
blocks.q: A country is building its first big factories and railroads, and savings and investment rise quickly. Which of Rostow's stages is this?
steps: Before it: preconditions (new ideas and institutions).
This burst of investment and industry is the take-off.
blocks.a: Take-off (stage 3).

blocks.html: Treating one theory as fact. Each explains some cases; scholars debate them, and many point out that countries have developed by different paths. On a test, describe each theory accurately and give a strength and a criticism.

blocks.html: Your phone may be designed in one country, use minerals from a second, chips from a third and be assembled in a fourth. Trade links places, often through the organizations above the state you studied. Economics covers the theory in Comparative Advantage.

Countries gain from trade by specializing in what they produce at the lowest opportunity cost: their comparative advantage (David Ricardo, 1817). Global supply chains, outsourcing and offshoring spread the steps of production around the world, often through special economic zones (Shenzhen, China, 1980) and export plants such as Mexico's maquiladoras (from 1965).

Even if one country is better at making everything, both can gain when each makes what it gives up the least to produce and trades for the rest. That is why a country can import goods it could make itself. Lower costs reach consumers as cheaper goods, and new factories bring jobs to places that need them. But trade also shifts work: some workers and towns lose jobs when production moves. Economists broadly agree that trade raises total income, and they debate how best to help those who lose.

head: Cloth per worker-day
Grain per worker-day
blocks.cap: Country A makes more of both. Who should make what?

blocks.title: Find the comparative advantage
blocks.q: Use the table. Which country has the comparative advantage in cloth?
steps: A: 1 ton of grain costs 2 rolls of cloth (6 ÷ 3), so 1 roll costs $1/2$ ton of grain.
B: 1 roll of cloth costs 1 ton of grain (2 ÷ 2).
A gives up less grain per roll ($1/2$ ton versus 1 ton).
blocks.a: Country A, in cloth. B has the comparative advantage in grain.

blocks.title: Zones and plants
blocks.q: A government sets aside an area near a port with lower taxes and simpler rules to attract foreign factories that export. What is it called, and what is one famous example?
steps: An area with special rules to attract investment and exports is a special economic zone.
China opened Shenzhen as one in 1980.
blocks.a: A special economic zone, such as Shenzhen.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Two famous export-manufacturing places: Shenzhen, China, and the maquiladoras of Mexico's border cities.

blocks.html: Thinking trade helps only one side. Trade can benefit both countries overall while some workers and places lose; economists agree on the overall gains and debate how to help those who lose. People also debate tariffs, labor standards and how much to rely on distant suppliers.

blocks.html: Development has raised incomes and lifespans, and it has also used resources and changed the environment, as you saw in human-environment interaction. Sustainable development asks how to keep improving lives without running down what future people will need.

Sustainable development is "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs" (the Brundtland Commission, Our Common Future, 1987). It has three pillars: environment, economy and society. In 2015 all UN members adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with 169 targets for 2030.

Theme

6 Clean water and sanitation; 7 Affordable and clean energy
8 Decent work and economic growth; 9 Industry, innovation and infrastructure; 10 Reduced inequalities; 11 Sustainable cities
12 Responsible consumption and production; 13 Climate action; 14 Life below water; 15 Life on land
16 Peace, justice and strong institutions; 17 Partnerships for the goals

Decent jobs and growth
Every child in school
Cleaner energy
Roads, ports and internet access
Equal opportunity for women and girls

blocks.cap: Sort goals into the three pillars. Many goals touch more than one.

blocks.html: Why tie the environment to poverty and education in one list? Because they depend on each other. Farms need healthy soil and water; schooling and health care raise incomes; growth pays for cleaner technology. A plan that helps one pillar while ruining another does not last. People do debate priorities and costs, such as how fast to change energy systems and who should pay, and the goals leave each country to choose its own path.

blocks.title: Which goal?
blocks.q: A city builds a bus rapid transit line and plants trees to cool hot neighborhoods. Which SDG does this serve most directly?
steps: It is about making a city work better for its people and environment.
That is Goal 11, sustainable cities and communities.
blocks.a: Goal 11, sustainable cities and communities.

blocks.title: Count the years
blocks.q: The SDGs were adopted in 2015 with targets for 2030. The Millennium Development Goals ran from 2000 to 2015. How long was each period?
blocks.a: 15 years each.

blocks.html: Thinking sustainability is only about the environment. The UN goals also cover poverty, health, education, equality and jobs. A sustainable plan has to work for all three pillars at once.
